title: ScopeCheck: An Air-Gapped Scope Creep & Contract Auditor for Freelancers
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built ScopeCheck is an offline, air-gapped auditor that evaluates client revision requests, late-stage change emails, and Statement of Work (SOW) terms without letting a single byte of client data leave your laptop. Almost every independent developer knows this exact message pattern near a milestone delivery: "The dashboard looks great! While you have the repo open, could you quickly wire up Stripe, user auth, and PDF export before tomorrow? It should only take a few minutes since the UI is done." When that lands in your inbox, you usually have two bad choices: Absorb 10+ hours of unbilled architectural labor just to keep the client happy. Draft a blunt, defensive response that strains the relationship right before milestone sign-off. Pasting a client's proprietary technical spec or signed contract into commercial cloud AI tools isn't an option either—doing so leaks unreleased business logic and breaches confidentiality agreements. ScopeCheck gives freelancers a safe third option. You paste the client's message into a local studio interface, and it gives you: A Severity Rating (1–10): An immediate diagnosis of how far the request steps outside standard delivery boundaries. Architectural Flagging: Calls out the actual technical debt hiding behind innocent wording (e.g., distinguishing between a CSS tweak and new database migrations or payment webhooks). A Pushback Draft: Generates a polite, firm negotiation script that validates the idea while framing additions as Phase 2 deliverables with separate pricing. Freelancers and boutique technical agencies lose thousands of dollars every year to unpaid scope creep. ScopeCheck catches that creep before work starts. Demo ScopeCheck runs locally via Ollama to guarantee client text never hits external servers. 1. Ingestion & Model Selection Paste raw emails, Slack messages, or contract clauses directly into the interface: 2. Breakdown & Negotiation Draft When auditing a typical "quick revision" asking for payment hooks and logins, the local engine flags the unbilled work and drafts a clear response: Code Razorbillworks / scopecheck Local, zero-leak scope creep and contract auditor for freelancers powered by Gemma. 🛡️ ScopeCheck An air-gapped, local contractual and scope-creep auditor built for freelance engineers, technical consultants, and boutique digital agencies. Powered by local Google Gemma inference via Ollama. Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 2 (Side Hustle Track) . The Real Problem with Freelance "Quick Revisions" Every independent developer or agency freelancer knows this exact message pattern: "The dashboard looks super clean! Hey, while you still have the codebase open, could you quickly wire up user authentication, Stripe webhooks, and an export-to-PDF button before tomorrow? Should only take a few minutes since the UI is already finished!" When this happens, freelancers are caught in a bad trade-off: Eat the cost: Do 10+ hours of unpaid architecture, backend plumbing, and QA to avoid an awkward confrontation. Burn the bridge: Send a blunt, defensive email that strains client relations right before milestone sign-off. Leak client data to cloud AI: Paste the… View on GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Razorbillworks/scopecheck License: Apache 2.0 How I Built It Local Reasoning Engine: Google Gemma ( gemma2:2b / gemma3:4b ). Gemma's instruction following is remarkably sharp at dissecting contract nuances and technical requirements without hallucinating clauses that don't exist. Runtime: Connected directly to Ollama via local loopback ( localhost:11434 ), eliminating external API calls and third-party prompt caching. Interface: Built with Python 3.10+ and Streamlit, styled with an editorial slate-obsidian layout designed for reading dense contracts cleanly. Prompt Architecture: The audit harness strictly separates risk calculation from diplomatic script drafting so the model doesn't blend technical debt with negotiation pleasantries. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Most side hustles and freelance agencies operate under strict non-disclosure agreements (NDAs). When you paste an unreleased product brief, API structure, or signed agreement into a proprietary cloud AI service, you lose control of that data. Closed platforms routinely log inputs, retain telemetry, and use prompts for future training cycles. For a contractor, that is an immediate legal liability. Open innovation is what makes an offline auditor viable: True Data Sovereignty: Gemma runs entirely inside your machine's RAM. Zero outbound network calls means client NDAs stay completely intact. Predictable Unit Economics: Closed APIs charge variable per-token fees that add up fast with long documents. A local open model costs exactly $0.00 to run. No Vendor Lock-In: You don't have to worry about sudden API rate limits, deprecations, or outages while traveling or working on restricted client networks. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma: ScopeCheck uses local Google Gemma models ( gemma2:2b / gemma3:4b ) as its primary analytical engine. Gemma's reasoning ability isolates technical deliverable creep, parses ambiguous client communications, and drafts commercial pushback scripts—all running efficiently on standard developer hardware.

title: One Request, Many Callers: Coalescing Duplicate fetch() Calls in JavaScript
body: Open the network tab of almost any single-page app and you'll find it: the same /api/me request fired three, five, sometimes ten times within a few milliseconds. The header wants the current user, so does the sidebar, the avatar, and the settings link. Every component calls fetch() independently, and none of them knows the others asked. On the server, the same thing happens when a cache entry expires and a hundred concurrent requests all miss it at once and hit the database together. That's the "thundering herd" (or "cache stampede") problem. The fix for both is request coalescing : while a request for a given key is in flight, every other caller gets the same promise instead of starting a new request. Data libraries like TanStack Query and SWR do this internally, but the core idea fits in about 40 lines, and understanding it helps you spot the edge cases those libraries handle for you. All code here runs unmodified on Node.js 20+ (which ships fetch globally) and in modern browsers. The naive version and its bugs The obvious implementation is a Map from URL to promise: const inFlight = new Map (); function naiveFetch ( url ) { if ( ! inFlight . has ( url )) inFlight . set ( url , fetch ( url )); return inFlight . get ( url ); } This has three problems: It never forgets. Entries stay in the map forever, so this is a memory leak that also serves stale data. A Response body can only be read once. If two callers both call res.json() on the same Response , the second one throws TypeError: Body is unusable: Body has already been read . Failures are cached. One network blip and that URL is broken until the page reloads. A correct version // coalesce.mjs export function createCoalescingFetch ({ ttlMs = 0 } = {}) { const inFlight = new Map (); // url -> Promise<{status, headers, body}> return async function coalescedFetch ( url , { signal } = {}) { let shared = inFlight . get ( url ); if ( ! shared ) { shared = ( async () => { const res = await fetch ( url ); const body = await res . text (); // read once, share the text if ( ! res . ok ) throw new Error ( `HTTP ${ res . status } for ${ url } ` ); return { status : res . status , headers : Object . fromEntries ( res . headers ), body }; })(); inFlight . set ( url , shared ); shared . then ( () => { if ( ttlMs > 0 ) setTimeout (() => inFlight . delete ( url ), ttlMs ). unref ?.(); else inFlight . delete ( url ); }, () => inFlight . delete ( url ) // never cache failures ); } if ( ! signal ) return shared ; // Let one caller give up without cancelling the request for everyone. signal . throwIfAborted (); return new Promise (( resolve , reject ) => { const onAbort = () => reject ( signal . reason ); signal . addEventListener ( " abort " , onAbort , { once : true }); shared . then ( resolve , reject ). finally (() => signal . removeEventListener ( " abort " , onAbort ) ); }); }; } Let's walk through the decisions. Read the body once, share the result. The shared promise resolves to a plain object containing the body text, not the Response . Every caller can read it as many times as they like. (Callers share the same object, so treat it as read-only, or Object.freeze it if you want that enforced.) Evict on settle. As soon as the request finishes, the entry is removed, so the next call goes to the network again. Coalescing is about de-duplicating concurrent work, not caching. If you do want a short cache, ttlMs keeps the settled promise around a little longer. The .unref?.() call stops that timer from keeping a Node.js process alive. In browsers, setTimeout returns a number, so the optional call simply does nothing. Never cache failures. The rejection handler deletes the entry immediately. Everyone who was already waiting gets the same error (which is correct, since they asked at the same moment), but the next caller retries. Isolate cancellation. This is the subtle one. If you passed a caller's AbortSignal into the shared fetch() , then the first component to unmount would cancel the request for every component. Instead, the shared request runs without a signal, and each caller races the shared promise against its own signal. A caller that aborts gets rejected right away, and everyone else is unaffected. Proving it works Claims about concurrency are cheap, so let's test them against a real HTTP server that counts how many requests it receives. The server waits 100 ms before responding, to give the callers time to overlap: // demo.mjs import http from " node:http " ; import assert from " node:assert/strict " ; import { createCoalescingFetch } from " ./coalesce.mjs " ; let hits = 0 ; let failNext = false ; const server = http . createServer (( req , res ) => { hits ++ ; setTimeout (() => { if ( failNext ) { failNext = false ; res . writeHead ( 503 ). end ( " busy " ); return ; } res . writeHead ( 200 , { " content-type " : " application/json " }); res . end ( JSON . stringify ({ path : req . url , hit : hits })); }, 100 ); }); await new Promise (( r ) => server . listen ( 0 , r )); const base = `http://127.0.0.1: ${ server . address (). port } ` ; Ten concurrent callers, one request: const get = createCoalescingFetch (); const results = await Promise . all ( Array . from ({ length : 10 }, () => get ( ` ${ base } /user/1` )) ); assert . equal ( hits , 1 ); assert . ok ( results . every (( r ) => r === results [ 0 ])); console . log ( " 10 callers -> " , hits , " request " ); Once settled, the next call is fresh, and different URLs are never merged: await get ( ` ${ base } /user/1` ); assert . equal ( hits , 2 ); console . log ( " after settle -> " , hits , " requests " ); await Promise . all ([ get ( ` ${ base } /a` ), get ( ` ${ base } /b` )]); assert . equal ( hits , 4 ); console . log ( " two urls -> " , hits , " requests " ); Failures are shared, then evicted: failNext = true ; const outcomes = await Promise . allSettled ([ get ( ` ${ base } /x` ), get ( ` ${ base } /x` )]); assert . equal ( hits , 5 ); assert . ok ( outcomes . every (( o ) => o . status === " rejected " )); const retry = await get ( ` ${ base } /x` ); assert . equal ( hits , 6 ); assert . equal ( retry . status , 200 ); console . log ( " failure shared then evicted -> " , hits , " requests " ); One caller aborting doesn't cancel the other: const ac = new AbortController (); const p1 = get ( ` ${ base } /slow` , { signal : ac . signal }); const p2 = get ( ` ${ base } /slow` ); setTimeout (() => ac . abort ( new Error ( " user navigated away " )), 20 ); const [ r1 , r2 ] = await Promise . allSettled ([ p1 , p2 ]); assert . equal ( r1 . status , " rejected " ); assert . equal ( r1 . reason . message , " user navigated away " ); assert . equal ( r2 . status , " fulfilled " ); assert . equal ( hits , 7 ); console . log ( " abort isolated -> " , hits , " requests " ); A short TTL turns it into a micro-cache: const cached = createCoalescingFetch ({ ttlMs : 500 }); await cached ( ` ${ base } /cfg` ); await cached ( ` ${ base } /cfg` ); assert . equal ( hits , 8 ); await new Promise (( r ) => setTimeout ( r , 600 )); await cached ( ` ${ base } /cfg` ); assert . equal ( hits , 9 ); console . log ( " ttl micro-cache -> " , hits , " requests " ); server . close (); console . log ( " all checks passed " ); Running it: $ node demo.mjs 10 callers -> 1 request after settle -> 2 requests two urls -> 4 requests failure shared then evicted -> 6 requests abort isolated -> 7 requests ttl micro-cache -> 9 requests all checks passed When to use it, and when not to Good fits: GET requests for data that many parts of the UI need at once (current user, feature flags, config) Server-side calls to upstream APIs or slow queries, where a cache miss under load would otherwise hit the backend once per concurrent request Expensive non-HTTP async work, too. Swap fetch(url) for any async function and the URL for any string key. Don't use it for: Non-idempotent requests. Two POST /orders calls are two orders. Never merge them. Requests that differ by more than the URL. If headers like Authorization or Accept-Language change the response, include them in the key. Otherwise user A can receive user B's data, which on a server is a security bug, not a performance bug. Streaming or huge responses. This version buffers the whole body into memory to share it. Takeaways Share the promise , not the Response , because a body can only be read once. Delete the entry when the request settles , and always on failure . Never let one caller's AbortSignal cancel shared work. Race it per caller instead. Build the cache key from everything that changes the response. Forty lines, no dependencies, and your network tab gets a lot quieter. Note: An AI assistant helped draft this post; all code was run and tested (Node.js 20.19).

title: Snaplist: A Local AI Listing Writer for Etsy & eBay Sellers (Gemma 3 + Ollama)
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built Snaplist is a listing writer for solo sellers on Etsy and eBay. You drop in a few photos of an item, pick a marketplace and a tone, add any facts the photos can't show (condition, size, backstory), and it drafts a title, a description, and up to 13 search tags. Every word is editable before you copy it out. Who would pay for it? Anyone who lists secondhand or small-batch items and keeps rewriting the same kind of description. The idea is a one-time desktop package rather than a monthly subscription. My working guess is around ₹999, but that is a pricing hypothesis I haven't tested, not revenue. Demo Video walkthrough, generating a listing from photos of a kitchen timer: https://youtu.be/j0H6ZO6grRg Code Public repo, MIT licensed: https://github.com/anshraj3060/snaplist How I Built It The core is Gemma 3 (4B) , an open-weight vision model, served by Ollama on my own MacBook Air. The app is a small Node.js server plus a browser UI. When you press Generate, the server sends your photos (base64) to Ollama's /api/chat endpoint and asks for structured JSON back, which the UI turns into an editable title, description, and tags. I built the app with an AI coding agent (Arena) from a prompt, then ran it myself: installed Ollama, pulled gemma3:4b , switched Snaplist from its labeled demo mode to "Use my local model", and tested it with my own photos. A few details I like: No silent fallback. If the model fails, you see an error, never fake sample text passed off as AI output. Demo mode is labeled "not AI generated" so nobody mistakes it for real analysis. The model is swappable. OLLAMA_MODEL=gemma3:12b npm start is all it takes to try a bigger one. Tags are capped at 13 and titles are limited per marketplace in code, not left to the model. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Cost structure. With open weights running locally, there is no per-listing API bill. That is what makes a one-time license even thinkable. A closed API would push me toward a subscription just to cover inference. Privacy. In local mode, photos go from the browser to the Snaplist server to Ollama, all on the seller's own computer. Unlisted products and supplier photos never reach a third party. Control. I can inspect the prompts, change the model with one environment variable, and later fine-tune for a niche. With a closed API I get whatever the vendor ships this month. Works offline. After the one-time model download, generation doesn't need the internet. Where it did not beat a closed model: a 4B model is small. In my first test I uploaded photos of four unrelated items, and it merged them into one confused listing. It did read a brand name off a bottle, which was a nice surprise. Descriptions come out short and need a human edit. CPU inference can be slow, and there is a 180-second timeout. Hardware and electricity still cost something, and Gemma is open-weight under its own terms, not OSI-approved open source. I also deliberately did not build price suggestions. Snaplist has no comparable-sales data, and I'd rather ship nothing than invent numbers. My First User I haven't had anyone else try it yet, so there is no first-user story to tell. Next step: put it in front of a real seller and ask what they'd pay, and what they'd want it to do next. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma : the whole project runs on Gemma 3 vision through Ollama.

title: Your Logs Are an API: Testing Python Logging with pytest's caplog
body: At 3 a.m., during an incident, your logs are the only interface you have to production. Dashboards, alerts, and log queries all depend on them: an alert fires on level=ERROR , a saved search filters on order_id , a compliance check makes sure no password ever reaches the log pipeline. That makes your log output an API . Other systems depend on its shape, yet most codebases never test it. Someone downgrades an error to a warning , renames order_id to orderId , or adds a debug line that dumps a whole request body, and no test fails. pytest has a built-in fixture for this, caplog . In this post we'll use it to test four things: The right level is used for the right situation Structured fields passed through extra= are present Unexpected errors carry a traceback A JSON formatter and a redaction filter behave correctly, together All code runs on Python 3.13 with pytest 9 and needs nothing beyond the standard library and pytest. The code under test Here is a small checkout function. It tells three different stories: a captured payment ( INFO ), a declined card ( WARNING , because it's a normal business outcome and shouldn't page anyone), and a gateway failure ( ERROR with a traceback, because it should). # checkout.py import logging logger = logging . getLogger ( " shop.checkout " ) class PaymentDeclined ( Exception ): pass def charge ( order_id , amount_cents , gateway ): logger . debug ( " charging order " , extra = { " order_id " : order_id }) try : gateway ( amount_cents ) except PaymentDeclined : logger . warning ( " payment declined " , extra = { " order_id " : order_id , " amount_cents " : amount_cents }, ) return False except Exception : logger . exception ( " gateway error " , extra = { " order_id " : order_id }) raise logger . info ( " payment captured " , extra = { " order_id " : order_id , " amount_cents " : amount_cents }) return True The extra= dictionary is the standard library's way of attaching structured fields. Each key becomes an attribute on the LogRecord , which is exactly what we'll assert on. Test 1: levels and fields caplog.records is a list of the actual LogRecord objects that were emitted. Asserting on records instead of formatted strings makes the tests resilient to formatting changes: import logging from checkout import PaymentDeclined , charge def ok_gateway ( amount ): return None def declining_gateway ( amount ): raise PaymentDeclined () def test_success_logs_info_with_order_id ( caplog ): caplog . set_level ( logging . INFO , logger = " shop.checkout " ) assert charge ( " ord-42 " , 1999 , ok_gateway ) is True [ record ] = caplog . records assert record . levelname == " INFO " assert record . getMessage () == " payment captured " assert record . order_id == " ord-42 " assert record . amount_cents == 1999 def test_decline_is_a_warning_not_an_error ( caplog ): caplog . set_level ( logging . INFO , logger = " shop.checkout " ) assert charge ( " ord-7 " , 500 , declining_gateway ) is False assert [ r . levelname for r in caplog . records ] == [ " WARNING " ] assert caplog . records [ 0 ]. order_id == " ord-7 " Two details matter here: caplog.set_level(..., logger=...) scopes the level change to one logger and restores it after the test, so tests don't leak configuration into each other. [record] = caplog.records is a small trick: the unpacking fails if there isn't exactly one record. That catches accidental duplicate logging, which is a common bug when a handler gets attached twice. The second test protects a decision that is easy to undo by accident. If someone "fixes" the decline path to use logger.error , your on-call rotation starts getting paged for expired credit cards. Now a test fails first. Test 2: debug output stays at debug Use the caplog.at_level context manager when a test needs different levels in different phases. caplog.messages gives you just the formatted message strings: def test_debug_line_only_appears_at_debug ( caplog ): with caplog . at_level ( logging . INFO , logger = " shop.checkout " ): charge ( " ord-1 " , 100 , ok_gateway ) assert " charging order " not in caplog . messages caplog . clear () with caplog . at_level ( logging . DEBUG , logger = " shop.checkout " ): charge ( " ord-1 " , 100 , ok_gateway ) assert caplog . messages [ 0 ] == " charging order " caplog.clear() resets the captured records between phases. Test 3: errors carry a traceback A log line that says gateway error without a stack trace is almost useless. logger.exception() attaches exc_info to the record, so assert that it's there and has the right type: import pytest def broken_gateway ( amount ): raise TimeoutError ( " gateway timed out " ) def test_unexpected_error_logs_traceback ( caplog ): caplog . set_level ( logging . ERROR , logger = " shop.checkout " ) with pytest . raises ( TimeoutError ): charge ( " ord-9 " , 100 , broken_gateway ) [ record ] = caplog . records assert record . exc_info is not None assert record . exc_info [ 0 ] is TimeoutError This test fails if someone replaces logger.exception(...) with logger.error(...) , which silently drops the traceback. Test 4: the formatter and the redaction filter Most production setups ship JSON logs. Here is a minimal formatter that copies every extra= field into the JSON, plus a filter that masks sensitive keys before anything is written: # app_logging.py import json import logging _RESERVED = set ( vars ( logging . makeLogRecord ({}))) | { " message " , " asctime " } SENSITIVE_KEYS = { " password " , " token " , " card_number " } class JsonFormatter ( logging . Formatter ): def format ( self , record ): payload = { " level " : record . levelname , " logger " : record . name , " message " : record . getMessage (), } # Anything passed via extra=... becomes an attribute on the record. for key , value in vars ( record ). items (): if key not in _RESERVED : payload [ key ] = value if record . exc_info : payload [ " exception " ] = self . formatException ( record . exc_info ) return json . dumps ( payload , default = str ) class RedactFilter ( logging . Filter ): def filter ( self , record ): for key in SENSITIVE_KEYS : if hasattr ( record , key ): setattr ( record , key , " [REDACTED] " ) return True The _RESERVED trick builds the set of attribute names every LogRecord has by default, so anything else on the record must have come from extra= . You can unit-test both classes without any logger at all, because logging.makeLogRecord() builds a record from a dict: import json from app_logging import JsonFormatter , RedactFilter def make_record ( ** extra ): return logging . makeLogRecord ( { " name " : " shop.checkout " , " levelname " : " INFO " , " levelno " : 20 , " msg " : " user %s logged in " , " args " : ( " alice " ,), ** extra } ) def test_formatter_emits_valid_json_with_extras (): line = JsonFormatter (). format ( make_record ( order_id = " ord-42 " )) data = json . loads ( line ) assert data == { " level " : " INFO " , " logger " : " shop.checkout " , " message " : " user alice logged in " , " order_id " : " ord-42 " , } @pytest.mark.parametrize ( " field " , [ " password " , " token " , " card_number " ]) def test_redact_filter_masks_sensitive_fields ( field ): record = make_record ( ** { field : " s3cret " }) assert RedactFilter (). filter ( record ) is True data = json . loads ( JsonFormatter (). format ( record )) assert data [ field ] == " [REDACTED] " assert " s3cret " not in json . dumps ( data ) Comparing the whole dict with == is deliberate. It catches extra fields leaking into the output, not just missing ones. Test 5: the whole pipeline Unit tests on the formatter are good, but the real bug is often in the wiring. caplog.handler is a real logging.Handler , so you can give it your production formatter and filter and assert on the final text with caplog.text : def test_full_pipeline_through_a_real_handler ( caplog ): logger = logging . getLogger ( " shop.checkout " ) caplog . handler . setFormatter ( JsonFormatter ()) caplog . handler . addFilter ( RedactFilter ()) caplog . set_level ( logging . INFO , logger = " shop.checkout " ) logger . info ( " login " , extra = { " user " : " alice " , " password " : " hunter2 " }) data = json . loads ( caplog . text . strip ()) assert data [ " user " ] == " alice " assert data [ " password " ] == " [REDACTED] " A fresh handler is created for every test, so this configuration doesn't leak into other tests. Running it $ python -m pytest -q ......... [100%] 9 passed in 0.01s Takeaways Assert on caplog.records , not strings. Records give you the level, the logger name, exc_info , and every extra= field as attributes. Use the [record] = caplog.records unpacking to catch duplicate log lines for free. Scope levels with set_level(..., logger=...) or at_level . Both restore the previous state automatically. Test redaction explicitly. A parametrized test over your sensitive keys is cheap insurance against a compliance incident. Test the wiring once by attaching your real formatter and filters to caplog.handler . If a dashboard, alert, or audit depends on a log line, that log line deserves a test. Note: An AI assistant helped draft this post; all code was run and tested (Python 3.13, pytest 9.1).

title: BLUF Meaning: Examples for ML Engineers and Data Scientists
body: Originally published on khadim.tech . In short: BLUF stands for bottom line up front. The first sentence of a message says what you need or what you concluded, and everything after it supports that sentence. In ML work, that means opening with the decision, the date or the business impact, and keeping metrics like ROC-AUC, the debugging story and tool names for later, or for the engineers who ask. Below are before-and-after examples for a production rollback, a delayed project, a GPU budget request, an A/B test, a client question, a chat message and an interview answer. I recently made BLUF the rule for everything I write at work: status updates, emails, merge request descriptions and chat replies. I work remotely, in a different time zone from most of the people who read my messages, so a message is usually read once, quickly, between other things. When the ask sits in the third paragraph, it waits until the next day. ML updates are especially easy to get wrong this way. The investigation is the part we find interesting, so that is where we start, and the reader has to get through the ROC-AUC numbers and the drift theory before finding out what we want from them. What does BLUF mean? BLUF stands for bottom line up front : put the conclusion, the recommendation or the request in the first sentence, and the supporting detail after it. The phrase comes from the US Army's correspondence regulation, AR 25-50, which tells writers to put the main point at the beginning and to use the active voice ( Wikipedia summarises the history ). Kabir Sehgal, writing about military email for Harvard Business Review , describes the BLUF as a short opening statement that "declares the purpose of the email and action required." His example from the US Air Force: BLUF: Effective 29 Oct 13, all Air Force Doctrine Documents (AFDDs) have been rescinded and replaced by core doctrine volumes and doctrine annexes. A reader who stops after that sentence knows what changed, from when, and that they need to switch documents. Anything after it is optional reading. The BLUF + SCR structure BLUF tells you where the point goes. For what comes after it, I use a short version of the Situation, Complication, Question framework from Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle , with the question replaced by the answer you are proposing: BLUF: what you need, or what you concluded, in one sentence a reader could act on Situation: one line of context the reader already agrees with Complication: what changed or what is blocking, in business terms Resolution: what you propose, by when, and what it gets them A short reply is just the first line. A decision request to a manager or client gets all four, and each one stays at a sentence or two. Good news has no complication, so you skip it. ML terms to cut, and what to say instead Executives and clients read for impact, timeline, cost, risk and the decision they need to make. Tool names and metrics belong in the message only when the reader asked for them or is an engineer who needs them. These are the translations I reach for most: Instead of Say ROC-AUC fell from 0.88 to 0.61 The model is now wrong on far more cases, and here is who that affects Precision is 0.74 About 1 in 4 cases we flag is a false alarm Data drift Customer behaviour has changed since the model was trained Overfitting It does well on the data it learned from and worse on new cases Hyperparameter tuning A week of tuning to improve accuracy p < 0.01 The result is very unlikely to be chance CUDA out of memory on the current GPUs Training needs a bigger machine, at a cost of X per month Retrain on fresh data Update the model with recent data, which takes N days BLUF examples for ML engineers and data scientists These scenarios are illustrative The situations and numbers in examples 1 to 6 are made up to show the shape. Swap in your real figures. Example 7 uses a real result from my own work. 1. A model is failing in production Before: I was looking at the logs for the fraud model and noticed ROC-AUC dropped from 0.88 to 0.61. I think it might be data drift, because marketing launched a new campaign that changed the input distributions... After: BLUF: I need approval to roll the fraud model back to version 2.1 by 2:00 PM to stop legitimate customers being blocked at checkout. Situation: Version 3.0 has been live for 48 hours. Complication: The new marketing campaign changed how customers behave, and accuracy has fallen 27%, so good transactions are being rejected. Resolution: Rolling back restores normal checkout immediately. We then retrain 3.0 on the new traffic, which takes 3 days. 2. A project is delayed by a data problem Before: We're blocked on the churn model. The upstream pipeline is broken and the schemas don't match, so my dataframe keeps throwing errors... After: BLUF: The churn prediction dashboard will slip one week, to November 15, unless the data pipeline is fixed today. Situation: We are building the model that tells sales which accounts are likely to leave. Complication: Last week's database migration dropped the timestamps from the activity logs, and training cannot run without them. Resolution: I have asked Data Engineering for a fix. If it lands today, we still deliver on November 8. 3. Asking for a GPU budget Before: Our workstations are too slow. Training takes four days because we're on older consumer GPUs and the batch size is capped. We should move to cloud GPU instances... After: BLUF: I'm requesting $3,500 a month for cloud GPUs, which brings the support assistant's launch forward by three weeks. Situation: We are training a support model to cut call-centre volume. Complication: Each training run takes 4 days on our current hardware, which pushes the launch past the holiday season. Resolution: Cloud GPUs cut a run to 3 hours. We launch three weeks earlier and save an estimated $20,000 in support costs. The before version argues for convenience. The after version prices the delay, which is what the person approving the money is weighing. 4. Reporting an A/B test win BLUF: I recommend moving the new recommendation model to 100% of traffic. In a two-week A/B test it lifted checkout conversion by 4.5%, at 99% confidence. Situation: The test split traffic evenly between the current model and the new one. Resolution: With your go-ahead, we deploy tomorrow morning. The projected gain is $12,000 a week. There is no complication line, because nothing went wrong. 5. A client asks "is the model ready?" Before: Validation mAP is at 0.91 now and recall on the defect class is 0.97. We still see some false negatives on small scratches, mostly under low lighting, so we're adding augmentation... After: Not for fully automatic rejection yet, but it is ready to flag parts for a human to check. In testing it catches 97 of every 100 defects, and the line needs 99 before it can run without a person. The misses are mostly small scratches in poor lighting. Two more weeks of data collection should close that gap, and I'll send the next numbers on the 30th. A client question gets an answer in the first word. "Not yet" with a usable alternative beats a page of metrics they have to interpret themselves. 6. A chat message Labels look stiff in chat, so keep the order and write it as plain sentences: Can't make Thursday 3 PM. Can we do Friday 11 AM instead? The GPU delivery moved to Thursday afternoon and I need to be there to sign for it. The request comes first, the alternative second, the reason last. 7. An interview answer Question: "Tell me about a time you improved a model in production." I improved our inference speed by 70% by moving model serving to TensorRT, ONNX and Triton. The context was an internal inference engine used across the ML team... The result is in the first sentence, and the story after it explains how. If the interviewer cuts you off after ten seconds, they already have the part that matters. Nobody says "BLUF" out loud in an interview; you just answer first. Should you write "BLUF:" in the message? In formal writing, such as status reports, escalations and decision requests, the label helps, as long as the readers know what it means. Sehgal drops the acronym in his corporate job because it would be unclear to his recipients, and starts with a bold "Bottom line:" instead. In chat, client messages and proposals I leave labels out entirely. The first sentence carries the bottom line and the rest is ordinary prose, because a message full of bold labels reads like a form. How I use BLUF in my own writing Every page on this site opens with an "In short" box that answers the page's question before the article starts. The SynthID test begins "Mostly, for what it is built to do," and then spends the rest of the page on the evidence. Search engines and AI answer tools quote passages, so a page with its conclusion in the first two sentences tends to be quoted with that conclusion attached. I also wrote the rule into the instructions my coding agent follows, so any message it drafts for me starts with the bottom line, and so do its reports back to me. The test I use is the same everywhere: if the reader stopped after the first sentence, would they know what I need from them? If you're preparing results for a stakeholder, or deciding whether a fine-tuned model is worth the effort, I'm happy to look at it with you. FAQ What does BLUF stand for? Bottom line up front. The term comes from US Army correspondence rules, which put the main point or recommendation at the start of a memo instead of the end. Outside the military it is used for email, status reports and any message where the reader may only read the first line. Should I write "BLUF:" at the top of the email? Only if your readers know the term. Kabir Sehgal, who wrote about military-style email for Harvard Business Review, starts his corporate notes with a bold "Bottom line:" instead, because the acronym would be unclear to his recipients. The order matters more than the label. What is the difference between BLUF and SCR? BLUF says where the main point goes: first. SCR (situation, complication, resolution) is a way to arrange the context that follows it. Together they give one sentence with the ask or conclusion, then a line each on the background, what changed, and what you propose. How do I explain model performance to non-technical stakeholders? Say what the metric changes for them: customers affected, revenue, cost, time or risk. "About 1 in 4 transactions we block belongs to a real customer" lands where "precision is 0.74" does not. Keep the metric ready for anyone who asks for it. Does BLUF work for good news? Yes. Lead with the decision the good news supports, such as moving a new model to all traffic, then give the result that justifies it. A good result sent without an ask often gets a thumbs-up and no decision. Disclosure: written with AI assistance, from my own notes and examples.

title: How to Build an LMS with Live Classes in Next.js
body: Originally published on the Aniq UI blog . By the end of this guide you will know how to build an online course platform with recorded lessons, live classes, quizzes, certificates and paid checkout, using Next.js, NestJS and the Learnio LMS template from Aniq UI. You will not have to build a student site, an admin panel and an API separately. We follow one example school from its first plan to launch. Each step names the screen or setting involved, and the commands come straight from the template's documentation. The same path works for a solo course creator, a training company, or an agency building an LMS for a client. About this example Ledgerline Academy is an illustrative business we use to show the steps. It is not a client story, and the numbers in it are examples, not results. The brief Ledgerline Academy is a small online school that teaches bookkeeping to people changing careers. Two instructors teach. The school wants to start with a few courses and grow. Here is what it needs: A free introductory course that anyone can take, so visitors can try the school before paying. Paid courses with recorded lessons, personal notes and downloadable worksheets. A live class every week for each cohort, held inside the platform instead of a separate meeting link. Quizzes with a pass mark, and assignments that an instructor marks with feedback. A certificate at the end of a course, with a page where an employer can check it. Two instructors who each manage only their own courses and students. An English and an Arabic version of the whole school. How the template covers the brief Need Where it lives What you use Free and paid courses Student site and API Course pages and checkout; a price of 0 skips payment entirely Course content Admin dashboard The curriculum builder with sections, lessons and draft or published states Notes and worksheets Student site The course player, with notes and downloadable resources per lesson Weekly live class Admin dashboard, student site, your meeting server Live classes, the course calendar, and a Jitsi Meet server you run Quizzes and assignments Admin dashboard and student site The quiz editor, assignment grading, graded on the server Certificates Student site Certificates page and the public verify page Instructors see their own courses Admin dashboard and API The Instructor role with an instructor profile linked to the account Taking payment API and student site Stripe Checkout and a signed webhook English and Arabic All three apps /en and /ar routes, message files, courses written in both languages Before you start: decisions to make Course platforms have a few decisions that are hard to undo once students and payments exist. Make them on paper first. Free, paid, or both? A course with a price of 0 enrolls the student immediately and never reaches a payment processor. A paid course goes through checkout and enrolls the student only after the processor confirms payment. Ledgerline uses both: a free intro to build trust, and paid courses behind it. Recorded, live, or both? The catalog can be filtered by live or recorded. Recorded courses need only lessons and a media bucket. Live courses also need a meeting server that you host. Decide whether live classes are part of launch, because the server is a separate piece of infrastructure with its own cost. Who teaches, and what may they touch? If one person does everything, you can use one super admin account. If you have several teachers, plan an instructor profile and a linked account for each. Which payment processors? The template supports Stripe cards and PayPal. The checkout always lists both, so plan to configure both before taking real money. If you want only one, plan a code change to the checkout. Which languages? English and Arabic ship ready. Course content holds exactly two languages: an English and an Arabic value for each title, description and lesson. A third interface language is possible, but a third content language means changes in the API and the admin editors. Where do video and files live? Course art, lesson video and handouts go to a Cloudflare R2 bucket or another S3-compatible store. Decide who owns the bucket and what you will do about backups. What do you tell people when they buy? Receipts and enrollment confirmations go through Resend, which needs a verified sending domain. Plan the domain and the sender address before you test email. Step by step Step 1: Choose the package Learnio is three apps: a student website, an admin and instructor dashboard, and a NestJS API behind both. You can buy them together as the Full Stack package, or one at a time. The student site alone runs on bundled sample data. The admin dashboard alone runs on an in-browser mock, and most of its screens stay empty until an API is connected. Ledgerline needs students, instructors and a database that all agree, so it takes the Full Stack package. If you already have an API, a single frontend can point at it. The commercial license covers unlimited projects, including work you deliver to a client. Look at the My templates page: pick the ZIP that matches the package you bought. What to check: the extracted folder for the full stack is learnio-lms , and it contains admin-dashboard , back-end , frontend and docker-compose.yml . Single-app packages extract to a folder of their own, with a Dockerfile , package.json and .env.example . Step 2: Run everything with Docker Download the ZIP from My templates, unzip it, and open a terminal in the learnio-lms folder. With Docker running, start the three apps: docker compose up --build The first start builds three images and seeds the database with demo data, so it takes a few minutes. Afterward the student site is at localhost:3030 , the admin at localhost:3031 , and the API at localhost:8000 . If a port is busy, add SITE_PORT , ADMIN_PORT or API_PORT to a .env file next to docker-compose.yml and run the command again. Three demo accounts let you see each side: a student ( demo@learnio.com , password Demo@123 ), a super admin ( admin@learnio.com , password Admin@123 ) and an instructor ( emily-davis@learnio.com , password Teach@123 ). Sign in as each one and click around before you change anything. Without Docker, you need Node.js 22 or 24, corepack enable , and one terminal per app, API first. This still shows the terminal opened inside the extracted folder, the place every command here assumes you are standing. Watch the build output: three images are built, and the two frontends hold back until the API reports healthy. The admin runs in its own terminal on port 3031 once the API is up. This is the administrator overview you should see after signing in as the super admin: cards and charts for the platform. What to check: open localhost:8000/api/health , which should answer with a status of ok, then sign in on each app with the demo accounts. If a page carries a notice about sample data, that app could not reach the API. What usually goes wrong: Docker is not running, or a port is taken. Free port 3030, 3031 or 8000, or set SITE_PORT , ADMIN_PORT or API_PORT . The first start seems stuck. It is seeding the demo data, and the frontends start only when the API is healthy. Yarn reports version 1.22. Run corepack enable and install again. A fresh run on a database you keep does not reset anything. docker compose down -v deletes the volume and the next start seeds fresh demo data. Step 3: Set the school's name, logo and colors The brand lives in files, and the student site and the admin keep separate copies, so change both: Student site: src/config/site.ts holds the name, description and social handles. src/config/brand.config.ts names the student dashboard. Admin: src/config/brand.config.ts holds the name, short name, company and the metadata base address. Logos: replace public/assets/brand/learnio-wordmark.png and learnio-mark.png with your own transparent PNGs at the same names. Colors: src/styles/theme-variables.css in each app, with light values under :root and dark values under .dark . The App Settings tab in the admin does not rebrand the apps. Its site_name and support_email only change the emails the API sends. Search both message folders for the old name in English and Arabic, and set the site's public address in NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL . What to check: change the name in both apps, rebuild, and look for the old name on the sign-in pages, in the footer and in the browser tab, in English and in Arabic. Replace the favicon and the sharing images too, since link previews use them. What usually goes wrong: only one of the two apps is rebranded, or the logo is stretched because its proportions differ from the declared size. If your artwork has another shape, update the declared width and height where the sidebar brand and the logo component set them. Step 4: Build the first course Open Courses in the admin and create the free intro course. Add sections, then lessons inside them, and drag to reorder. A lesson can be a video, a reading, a quiz or an assignment. Attach worksheets as lesson resources, and leave the course as a draft until it is ready. Only published public courses reach the catalog. Titles, descriptions and lessons are stored once with an English and an Arabic value, and the editors give you a tab for each. Ledgerline writes both before publishing. A free course has a price of 0 and needs no payment processor at all. Uploads (video, handouts, course art) go to a Cloudflare R2 or other S3-compatible bucket once you set the five R2_* variables in back-end/.env . Until then the demo's bundled sample files still play, and only new uploads fail. Build it in this order: Create the course with its title, description, price and category, in both languages. Add sections, then lessons inside each section, choosing a lesson type. Attach worksheets and handouts to the lessons that need them. Flag a lesson as a free preview if you want visitors to see a sample. Only free-preview lessons expose their content and video on the public course page. Publish the course when it is ready. Until then it stays a draft and the public API answers not found. Look at how sections hold their lessons, each with a handle you drag to change the order. What to check: open the public course page in another browser. It should show the overview, syllabus, price and the enroll action. Then sign in as the demo student and open the course player to see lessons, notes and resources. What usually goes wrong: a course is visible in the admin but not on the site because it is still a draft or is not set to public. Another common one is a missing Arabic title, which makes the Arabic page fall back to empty fields. Step 5: Add quizzes, assignments and certificates In the quiz editor, add questions and answer options, then set a passing score and an attempt limit, or allow unlimited attempts for practice. The server grades every attempt, so students cannot change a score in the browser. Required quizzes count toward finishing the course. Assignments appear in the student's calendar, where they hand in a submission. The instructor opens the submissions, saves a grade, and writes feedback for that student. After every finished lesson and every passed quiz, the API re-checks whether the course is complete. When it is, the enrollment is marked complete, a certificate is issued and the student gets a notification. Anyone can then check a certificate number at /en/verify-certificate , with no account. Look at the submission waiting to be marked: the instructor sets a grade and writes feedback addressed to that student. What to check: take a quiz as the demo student and fail it on purpose, then pass it. Confirm the attempt limit stops you when it should. Submit an assignment from the calendar, mark it as an instructor, and look for the notification on the student side. What usually goes wrong: a required quiz is left unpassed, so the certificate is not ready, and the student is told so. Also check that the passing score is a number the questions can actually reach. Step 6: Take payments in test mode Out of the box the checkout uses a built-in simulator. It contacts no processor and charges nobody, and a card number that ends in 0 is rejected, which lets you rehearse a failed payment. Run a full purchase this way first, as the demo student. To move to Stripe, create test keys in your Stripe account and put STRIPE_SECRET_KEY , STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET in back-end/.env . Then add a webhook endpoint in Stripe that points at your API's address followed by /api/webhooks/payments/stripe . A student is enrolled when the webhook confirms the payment, not when they return to the site. Without the webhook, orders stay pending. PayPal has its own keys: PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID , PAYPAL_CLIENT_SECRET , PAYPAL_WEBHOOK_ID and PAYPAL_ENV . Read the warning in the mistakes section below before you go live. This is the checkout a student sees: choose card or PayPal, and the form follows the method you picked. What to check: buy a paid course three ways. First on the simulator, to confirm the seat appears. Then decline a payment with a card number that ends in 0 and confirm no seat is granted. Then, once Stripe test keys are in, buy again and confirm the order moves from pending to paid after the webhook arrives. The order page in the admin shows each order with its course, method and status. What usually goes wrong: The order stays pending. The webhook endpoint address is wrong, or STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET does not match that endpoint. A signed-out visitor presses pay and is sent to sign in. Paying needs a student account. The wrong processor handles a test. A method with no keys still runs the simulator. Step 7: Set up live classes Live classes run on a Jitsi Meet server that you host. The template does not include one, and the hosting cost is yours. Without it, the calendar shows live classes as unavailable. Put the server's details in back-end/.env (the example file lists the variables), and the API issues the tokens that let students and instructors into the room. An instructor schedules a session from the dashboard, and it appears in the course calendar next to assignment deadlines. Students open it from /en/dashboard/calendar . The room opens shortly before the start time, with a prejoin screen first, and the instructor gets host controls. Ledgerline schedules one session per week per cohort. Look at how live sessions and assignment deadlines share one calendar, so a student sees the whole week in a single place. What to check: schedule a session as an instructor, then open the student calendar and confirm the class appears. Open the class page close to its start time and confirm the room becomes available. What usually goes wrong: the calendar marks classes unavailable because no meeting server is configured, or the room is opened too early. The room opens shortly before the class, not when it is scheduled. Step 8: Add instructors with the right limits Students and staff sign in at different endpoints and receive tokens that only their own routes accept. The seed creates six staff roles: Super Admin, Admin, Manager, Editor, Viewer and Instructor. The Instructor role covers live classes, assignments, curriculum, and course editing, plus a read of students, enrollments and reviews. The key detail is the link between an admin account and an instructor profile. A linked account is also limited to its own courses: it sees only those courses and their students, and any attempt to write elsewhere gets a 403. The seeded emily-davis@learnio.com account shows the setup. Ledgerline creates both instructors this way, and keeps the super admin for the owner. What to check: sign in as the instructor and confirm the course list shows only that instructor's courses. Then try to change another instructor's course and confirm the change is refused. What usually goes wrong: an instructor sees too much because the account is not linked to an instructor profile. Or the reverse: a teacher cannot create lessons because the role lacks the curriculum permission. Edit the role on the roles screen and the change reaches signed-in staff. Step 9: Connect email and, if you want, the AI assistant Verification links, password resets, receipts and enrollment confirmations go out through Resend, in English and Arabic. Put your RESEND_API_KEY in back-end/.env and verify a sending domain with Resend. Without a key nothing breaks: each message is printed in the API log instead, which is handy while testing. The admin dashboard also has an AI assistant. It can look up courses, instructors and enrollments, turn a single request into a course draft, including the Arabic title and description, schedule classes and draw registration charts. It runs on a Google, OpenAI or DeepSeek key that you pay for. With no key in back-end/.env , it asks the admin for a key in the browser. Treat what it creates as a draft and review it before publishing. The chat shows a single request turned into a draft course, which an admin then reviews and edits like any other course. What to check: trigger a receipt by buying a paid course, then look in your inbox. Ask the assistant for a small draft course and open the result in the course editor to confirm both languages were filled. What usually goes wrong: email goes nowhere because the key is missing or the domain is not verified. Until a key exists, messages appear in the API log. The assistant also does not work on the admin's offline sample data. Step 10: Go live Generate a secret with node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))" and use it as JWT_SECRET . In back-end/.env set NODE_ENV=production , CORS_ORIGIN (list both frontend addresses, separated by commas) and FRONTEND_URL (the student site). In each frontend's .env set NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL with /api on the end, set NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL to the real domain, and rebuild. These values are compiled in. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_BASE_URL in the admin so live notifications work. If you use R2, add your bucket's public host as NEXT_PUBLIC_MEDIA_HOSTNAME (or MEDIA_HOSTNAME with Compose) and rebuild. Change the published demo passwords, or start from empty tables. For MySQL, create an empty database, set the driver and connection in back-end/.env , and run yarn seed . On a live site, yarn db:sync creates the tables without writing any rows. What to check after going live: make a real test purchase with a small amount or a discounted course, watch the order settle, confirm the enrollment email arrives, and verify the certificate page opens for someone who is not signed in. What usually goes wrong: The API refuses to start with an example JWT_SECRET or an empty CORS_ORIGIN , and prints what to fix. A frontend still shows the sample data notice, because its API address was missing at build time. Checkout rejects a purchase from a page in a language the API does not list. Add the language to both sides before opening it. Running it day to day After launch, Ledgerline's team works from a handful of screens. Watching the platform The overview shows cards and charts for the platform. Admins also receive notifications when a student is given a seat, finishes a course, leaves a review, registers, or when a course is published. An instructor hears only about their own courses. Marking and replying Instructors open the submissions waiting to be marked, save a grade, and leave feedback. Students and instructors keep a conversation per course, with history and image attachments, and an unread indicator. Looking after orders Each order carries a status of pending, paid, failed or refunded, and a gateway that names the processor, the built-in simulator, or a free course. Revenue figures leave free orders out of the average order value, so a free intro does not drag it down. If you need to add a seat that was paid for elsewhere, an admin can record it by hand. An order page like this shows the course, the payment method and the payment status in one place. Moderating reviews Reviews move through published, pending and hidden. If you set reviews_require_approval to true, new reviews stay pending until someone with moderation rights publishes them. Each change updates the course rating and the instructor rating. People and recycle bins Deleting a student, instructor, course, category, review or post moves it to a recycle bin where it can be restored, so a slip is not permanent. An example launch plan by week This schedule is an example for Ledgerline, not a promise about how long your launch will take. Week 1, understand. Run the stack, sign in as each role, and settle the decisions list. Week 2, brand and first course. Rebrand both apps and build the free intro course in both languages. Week 3, assessment and payments. Add quizzes, assignments and certificates, then test purchases on the simulator and with Stripe test keys. Week 4, live classes and staff. Stand up the meeting server, create the instructor accounts, and run a trial class with colleagues. Week 5, production. Set the production environment, connect email, rebuild the frontends, and make one real purchase. Week 6, soft launch. Open the free course first, then the paid ones. Launch checklist Names, logos, icons and colors replaced in both apps, plus sharing images. Courses published in both languages, with prices set. Quizzes have reachable passing scores, and required quizzes are marked. Stripe and PayPal both configured, with webhook subscriptions in place. A real test purchase completed and an enrollment email received. Meeting server running and a trial class held. Instructor accounts linked to instructor profiles and tested. JWT_SECRET , CORS_ORIGIN and FRONTEND_URL set for production. Frontend API addresses, site address and media host set, then rebuilt. Published demo passwords changed or removed. Resend domain verified. Backups planned for the database and the media bucket. Privacy and terms pages reviewed for your own business. Template, from scratch, or a hosted course platform A hosted course platform You can have a school online quickly, with hosting, video and payments handled for you. The price is ongoing fees, limits on layout and workflow, and student data on someone else's system. It is a good fit when you want to teach and do not need custom behavior. Building from scratch You decide everything. You also build accounts for two audiences, a curriculum editor, a lesson player, quizzes, grading, certificates, checkout with webhooks, email, live class tokens and two languages before you teach your first lesson. Starting from a template You get those pieces already wired, with source code you own and can change. You host it, update it and fill the gaps that this guide names: a meeting server, your own payment accounts, a mail domain. It fits a school that wants its own brand and rules, or an agency building the platform for a client. What it costs to run Learnio packages start from $79 for a single app, and the Full Stack package Ledgerline uses is $179. It comes with a commercial license and lifetime support. The rest is what you switch on: Hosting for the three apps, and a database if you move past SQLite. Stripe and PayPal charge their own processing fees. See Stripe's pricing page and the PayPal merchant fees page. Resend for email, plus a domain you can verify. A Jitsi Meet server for live classes, with its own hosting cost. An S3-compatible bucket such as Cloudflare R2 for video and files. An AI key, only if you use the assistant. Local work is free. SQLite needs no database server, the checkout simulator charges nobody, and free courses never need a processor. What to customise next Categories and the catalog. Set the catalog page size with the courses_per_page setting. Review moderation. Set reviews_require_approval to true so new reviews wait for a moderator. Blog. The admin has a blog editor, and the student site publishes the posts. It is a quiet way to bring in search traffic. Default language. Open in Arabic by setting defaultLocale to ar . A third language. Add a locale to each app and the API. Course content itself holds exactly two languages. Roles. Edit what each role may do on the roles screen and the change reaches signed-in staff. Common mistakes Skipping the webhook If students pay and nothing happens, the webhook is the first thing to check. Enrollment follows the processor's confirmation, so a missing subscription leaves orders pending. Configuring Stripe but not PayPal The checkout always offers card and PayPal. An order paid through a method with no keys uses the simulator and completes without charging anyone. Configure both before you take real orders. Expecting live classes without a meeting server The template provides the scheduling, tokens and room screens. The meeting server is yours to run. No server means the calendar marks classes as unavailable. Broken course images after connecting a bucket A frontend shows pictures only from hosts that were listed when it was built. Add your bucket's public host, with no https:// , and rebuild. Treating App Settings as a rebrand The tab changes the emails only. Names, logos and colors come from files in each app. FAQ How do I build an LMS with Next.js? Start from a template that already covers courses, progress, assessment and payment, then adapt the brand and content. Learnio gives you a Next.js 16 student site, an admin dashboard and a NestJS API that already work together. Does it support live classes? Yes, on a Jitsi Meet server that you run. Students and instructors join inside the platform, from a course calendar that also shows deadlines. Can I use it for clients? Yes. The license covers unlimited projects, including ones you hand over to a customer. You cannot resell the source code or release it as a template. Does it support Arabic and RTL? Yes. All three apps ship in English and Arabic, and Arabic runs right to left. Course content is entered in both languages. Do I need a backend? For a real school, yes. The frontends can run alone on sample data, but accounts, payments and progress need the API, which comes in the Full Stack and Backend API packages. Can I sell courses with PayPal as well as Stripe? The template includes PayPal integration code and a PayPal webhook route next to Stripe's. Both need your own accounts and keys. Can I offer free courses? Yes. A course priced at 0 enrolls the student straight away and never reaches a payment processor. Can instructors see only their own courses? Yes. An account linked to an instructor profile is limited to that instructor's courses and their students, and writes outside them are refused. What happens when a payment fails or is refunded? The processor's webhook events settle, fail or refund the order. The seat is created only when the payment is confirmed, so a failed payment never grants one. Can I add another language? Yes, for the interface. Add the code to the student site's locale list, to the admin's lists and to the API's supported list, then translate the message files. Course content itself holds only English and Arabic. Try it yourself Open the student website demo and the admin and instructor demo . Then read the Learnio documentation or visit the Learnio product page . More options are in the education and LMS templates category and the best Next.js templates guide . Learnio is also one of the ten templates in the Next.js Templates Bundle .

title: I Built a Private AI Bookkeeper for Freelancers — Without Depending on a Proprietary AI API
body:
Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Submission 💸
tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge, ai, opensource
This is a submission for the "Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle" ( https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week2-2026-10-12 ).
Your Invoices Are Nobody Else’s Business: Building a Local-First AI Bookkeeper
Imagine finishing a month of freelance work, opening a folder full of invoices and receipts, and realizing that your next task is to manually organize every single document.
Extract the vendor name. Find the invoice date. Identify the total. Categorize the expense. Check for missing information.
For freelancers and small business owners, this is the kind of administrative work that quietly eats into time they could spend doing actual work.
AI can help automate it. But what if the documents contain sensitive financial information? And what happens when the cost of using an AI API starts eating into the savings from automation?
That got me thinking: Can I build a useful AI bookkeeping assistant that gives freelancers more control over their data, their costs, and the technology they depend on?
That’s the idea behind BillBuddy Local, my project for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.
The project is currently in development, and this is the problem I’m setting out to solve.
BillBuddy Local is a planned privacy-first AI assistant that helps freelancers, independent consultants, and small businesses turn invoices and receipts into organized financial records.
Instead of manually copying information from document to spreadsheet, the goal is to make the process as simple as uploading a document and reviewing the extracted information.
The goal isn't to replace accountants or let an AI make financial decisions without supervision.
It's to eliminate repetitive data entry while keeping people in control of their records.
I'm starting with a specific audience: freelancers, solo consultants, independent creators, and small agencies that regularly handle invoices but don't need an expensive enterprise accounting platform.
The business model I'm exploring is a free local version, with potential paid features such as batch processing, team workflows, additional export formats, and optional hosted deployment.
My initial pricing hypothesis is ₹299–₹799 per month, depending on the features and usage limits.
That price isn't validated yet. One of my goals is to get the product in front of potential users and find out whether the time saved is valuable enough for them to pay for it.
A side hustle needs more than a clever technical implementation. It needs a problem people actually want solved.
I'm working toward an end-to-end demo that shows a sample invoice being processed, the extracted fields being reviewed, and the final record being exported.
I'll add the working demo link here once the application is ready.
GitHub repository: "Fiza-Naaz339/BillBuddy"
I'm developing the project in the open so that the implementation, technical decisions, and future improvements can be inspected and reproduced.
As development progresses, I'll document the setup instructions, model configuration, sample documents, and tests needed to run the application.
I don't want BillBuddy Local to be another chatbot that simply reads a document and returns a paragraph.
I want to build a document-processing pipeline where each component has a clear responsibility.
These are the technologies and architectural choices I'm working toward; the complete pipeline is not implemented yet.
One principle I want to follow throughout the build is that the language model shouldn't be responsible for everything.
OCR can handle text recognition. The model can interpret the extracted text and propose structured fields. Deterministic code can validate predictable rules. The user can resolve uncertainty.
Separating these responsibilities should make the system easier to test, debug, and improve.
A polished interface isn't enough to prove that an AI document-processing tool is useful.
Once the pipeline is implemented, I want to evaluate it against a set of manually verified invoices and receipts.

I'd also like to compare the chosen open-weight model against a baseline using the same documents and evaluation rules.
I haven't collected these results yet. I'd rather measure actual performance than claim improvements based on assumptions.
For this project, open innovation isn't just a technology preference. It could change the economics and privacy options available to the people using the product.
Invoices and receipts can contain personal information, business relationships, addresses, and tax details.
My goal is to support a local-first workflow in which document processing can happen on hardware controlled by the user.
That requires more than running the language model locally. OCR, storage, logs, and other processing must also be configured appropriately if the entire workflow is to remain local.
For users who prefer a hosted experience, deployment and data-handling choices will need to be clearly documented.
A product aimed at freelancers needs sustainable economics.
If every processed invoice requires a paid proprietary API call, the cost structure depends partly on another provider's pricing and usage limits.
An open-weight model gives me the option to investigate local inference or self-managed hosting, depending on the model's hardware requirements and the needs of the customer.
Open-source AI isn't automatically free. Hardware, hosting, maintenance, and development still have costs. The advantage is having more flexibility over how those costs are managed.
Different models have different strengths, resource requirements, and performance characteristics.
An open-weight approach gives me room to evaluate alternatives, experiment with inference runtimes, and optimize the pipeline for the invoice formats my users actually encounter.
If a smaller model provides sufficient accuracy at lower operating cost, I can investigate using it. If a model struggles with certain documents, I can compare alternatives using the same evaluation set.
The goal is to choose based on evidence rather than being locked into one provider's ecosystem.
Invoices vary across vendors, industries, and countries.
An open codebase could allow other developers to contribute document parsers, validation rules, language support, integrations, and evaluation datasets.
I want this project to be something developers can inspect, learn from, and adapt to their own use cases.
For me, open innovation means more than making source code available. It means giving people the flexibility to understand and improve the tools they rely on.
My immediate priority is to turn the idea into a working end-to-end application.
The final step matters just as much as the technical work.
I want to find out whether the application actually saves time, which errors users care about most, and which features would make it useful enough to pay for.
I don't have a validated customer or measured performance results to share yet. Those are things I want to earn through implementation and real-world testing.
My measure of success won't be how many AI features I can fit into the application.
