title: How to Build a SaaS Admin Panel With an AI Assistant in Next.js
body:
Originally published on the Aniq UI blog . By the end of this guide you will have an internal admin panel with an AI assistant running on your computer and ready for a server. It is a Next.js dashboard with its own API behind it, and you build it from the Aniq UI Admin Dashboard Template 2 instead of starting from an empty folder. The steps work for a SaaS admin panel, a back office for a small company, or any internal tool where a team needs lists, roles and a way to ask questions about their own data. To keep it concrete, we walk one made-up company through the whole job, from the first download to a live address, and we stop at every point where something usually goes wrong. About this example Larkspur Software is an illustrative business we use to show the steps. It is not a client story, and the numbers in it are examples, not results. Before you start: decisions to make Most of the pain in an internal tool comes from choices made late. Settle these six before you open a terminal, and the rest of the guide goes faster. Who signs in, and what may each person do? Write the list of roles on paper first. The template ships five (Super Admin, Admin, Manager, Editor, Viewer) and you can reshape them, but it is easier to reshape with a plan. What are your records? The template comes with users, projects, tasks and app settings. If your business revolves around something else, such as orders or tickets, decide now whether you will rename what exists or add a new module to the API. Which languages? English and Arabic ship. A third language is possible but is more work, so know before you start whether you need it. Who pays for AI? Either the company holds one provider key on the server, or each person brings their own. The choice changes your bill and your privacy story, and step 8 covers both. Where will it run? A single small server using Docker, or Vercel for the dashboard with the API on a Docker host. Pick the shape early so you set the right addresses once. Which database? SQLite is the default and needs no setup. MySQL is a configuration change. A host without a persistent disk is the usual reason to pick MySQL. The brief Larkspur Software is a small agency that builds web apps for other companies. The office needs one place to run its work. Here is what the team asks for: A sign-in for staff, with different levels of access: the owner sees everything, developers edit projects, contractors only read. A list of every client project, with its status, its environment (staging or production) and its current version. A list of client accounts, with a quick way to find the ones who never verified their email. An assistant that answers plain questions such as "which projects are blocked?" and shows the answer as a table or a chart. English and Arabic, because two client teams read Arabic. A first run on a laptop, then a small server on the agency's own domain. Control over who can use the assistant, since it can change records and the AI provider bills for usage. How the template covers the brief Need Where it lives What you use Staff with different access Dashboard and API Admin Management and Admin Roles screens; permissions named like projects.edit Client project tracking Dashboard and API Projects screen with status, environment, version and an English and Arabic name Client accounts Dashboard and API Users and Deleted users screens, filters, verify and restore actions Plain-language questions Dashboard and API AI Assistant screen, with a provider key from you English and Arabic Dashboard /en and /ar addresses, message files under messages/ Laptop, then a server Docker and configuration Docker Compose, .env files, a web server in front Control over the assistant API The ai_chat.use permission on a role `` `` Template, from scratch or a hosted builder There are three honest ways to get an admin panel with an AI assistant, and each fits a different team. From scratch. You get exactly the structure you want and nothing extra. You also build sign-in, roles with live updates, filtered lists, a chat interface that renders tables and charts, and the API behind all of it. This suits teams with an unusual product and plenty of engineering time. For everyone else it means a long stretch spent on screens that every admin panel needs. A hosted builder. A low-code or internal-tool service gets you a working screen quickly and handles hosting for you. In exchange you work inside its component set and its pricing model, and moving away later usually means rebuilding. Check what it charges per user, what you can export, and whether it supports right-to-left layouts before you commit. A template with source code. You start with finished screens, a working API and an assistant, and you own the code. You pay once for the template, host it yourself, and change anything you like. The cost is that you must be comfortable with Next.js, and later with NestJS if you extend the API. The license does not let you publish or resell the source, but it does cover unlimited projects, including ones for clients. Larkspur has developers on staff and wants to keep client data on its own server, so it takes the template route. If nobody on your team writes code, a hosted builder is the more realistic choice. An example launch plan by week This is a sample schedule for Larkspur, not a benchmark. Your own pace will differ. Week 1, get it running. Download the ZIP, start it with Docker, click through every screen, and try both sample accounts. Decide the six questions above. Week 2, make it theirs. Brand it, rebuild the roles, create the real staff accounts, and delete the sample admins. Week 3, load the work. Enter real projects and client accounts, add provider keys, and let two or three people use the assistant with real questions. Week 4, harden and ship. Set production environment values, deploy to the server, check the health address, and walk through the launch checklist near the end of this post. Step by step 1. Choose the package The template comes in three packages. The Full Stack package holds the dashboard and the NestJS API. The Admin Dashboard package is the dashboard alone, running against a small mock server built into it, with the sample records stored in your browser. The Backend API package is the API alone. Larkspur wants real data and a real assistant, so it takes Full Stack. If you only want to design screens first, the Admin Dashboard package is enough, and you can point it at an API later. If you already have a front end and only need the server, the Backend API package gives you the routes, the roles logic and the assistant's tools. Check: after the download, your account should show a ZIP named for the package you bought. Usually goes wrong: buying the dashboard package and expecting an API in it. The dashboard alone cannot store anything outside the browser. 2. Run it locally with Docker Install Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine on Linux) and nothing else. Then work through these sub-steps. 2a. Download. Open My templates in your Aniq UI account and download the Full Stack ZIP. Look at which package is chosen on the download page, because the folder names in the later steps depend on it. 2b. Unzip and open the folder. Unpack the archive and start a terminal inside the dashboard-2-full-stack folder (on Windows, unpack it with File Explorer first). Look at the folder contents: you should see back-end , front-end and docker-compose.yml side by side. 2c. Start both apps. bash docker compose up --build On the first start Docker builds two images and seeds the database, so give it a few minutes. Later starts take seconds. Look at the terminal: it prints build progress first, and the dashboard waits until the API reports itself healthy. 2d. Open it. Go to localhost:3030 and use the account admin@example.com with the password Admin@123 . Arabic lives at /ar . The API answers at localhost:8000/api/health once its database is ready. What to check: the health address should answer, and the dashboard should list data on its first screen. What usually goes wrong: a port is already in use. If another program holds 3030 or 8000, create a file named .env next to docker-compose.yml and set DASHBOARD_PORT=3040 (or API_PORT for the API), then run the same command again. A start that seems stuck is normally still seeding sample data. To stop the apps, press Ctrl+C. Your data stays in a Docker volume. Be careful with docker compose down -v : the -v deletes the volume, and the next start brings back fresh sample data. 3. Know the other ways to run it You will not use all of these, but each solves a real situation. The dashboard alone. With the Admin Dashboard package, you build one image and start one container. With no API address set, it runs on its mock server and needs no back end. Look at the folder name in the terminal: this package extracts to a different folder than the Full Stack one. Look at the build output: the dependencies and the build both happen inside the image, so the first build needs an internet connection. The API alone. With the Backend API package, you build an image and run it with a volume that holds the database file. The first run seeds that database with the sample records and accounts. Every route sits under /api , and you check it with the health address. Look at the files in the folder, which include a Dockerfile , package.json and .env.example . Look at the image being built: the API image is separate from the dashboard's. Look at the health check at the end: a working API answers with an ok status. Without Docker. Install Node.js 22.9 or newer and run corepack enable once. Start the API first, because the dashboard reads all its data from it. In back-end , copy the example settings, create the database with yarn seed , then run yarn dev . In front-end , copy the example settings and start it the same way. Look at the first terminal, which runs the API. Look at the second terminal, which runs the dashboard against the API from the first. The same approach works for the single-app packages. Look at how little is needed here: no .env file means the mock server answers. Look at the API terminal staying open while you use it. What usually goes wrong: a Node.js older than 22.9, which makes yarn dev fail on reading .env ; a Yarn that answers with version 1.22 because Corepack is off; and a dashboard that shows sample data even though you meant to use your API, because the API address was missing when it was built. 4. Explore the sample data before you change anything The seed loads a small company's worth of records: a dozen admins, five roles carrying 25 permissions, 15 users, 15 projects, 10 tasks and 13 app settings, plus some deleted users and projects to practise restoring. Click through the sidebar from top to bottom, ending on the page that lists every UI component. Look at how the sidebar groups the screens, since you will rename and prune this menu later. Look at the top of the overview: key figures, charts, a calendar and quick tasks share one screen, and the widgets can be rearranged. Then sign out and sign in as john.smith@admin.com with the password admin123 . This account has the Viewer role. It can read every list but cannot create, edit or delete anything, and it cannot open the assistant. Seeing that difference early tells you how the permission system behaves, which matters for step 6. What to check: you can explain, in one sentence each, what Super Admin and Viewer can do. What usually goes wrong: people edit sample records first and then forget which data is real. Keep the sample data untouched until you are ready to replace it in bulk. 5. Put the agency's name on it All branding sits in the dashboard folder ( front-end in the Full Stack package). Run yarn dev there while you edit and the page reloads on every save. Four places matter most: src/config/brand.config.ts holds BRAND_CONFIG : the name, the company, the page metadata and the installed-app details, in English and Arabic. public/assets/images/logo-for-lightmode.png and logo-for-darkmode.png are the two logos. Replace the files and keep the names. src/styles/theme-variables.css defines every colour once for light and once for dark. The brand colour is --primaryColor . messages/
/en.json and ar.json hold every word on screen. Edit both languages together. Larkspur changes the name, swaps both logos and picks one new primary colour. That is enough for the dashboard to feel like theirs. Components read colours through variables such as bg-[var(--surface)] , so any component you add later keeps both themes if it does the same. Look at the component page: it is the quickest way to see your new colour on every kind of control at once. What to check: switch between light and dark in the header, then open the component page in both. What usually goes wrong: a logo with a baked-in background colour that looks wrong in one theme. Export both logos with transparent backgrounds. 6. Set up staff and roles The seed ships five roles: Super Admin, Admin, Manager, Editor and Viewer. One person can carry more than one role, and they receive the combined permissions of all of them. Permissions are named module.action , for example users.view , projects.edit or settings.edit , and there are 25 of them across admins, roles, users, projects, settings and the assistant. Larkspur maps its team like this: the owner stays Super Admin, the two project leads become Manager, developers become Editor, and contractors become Viewer. Do it in three passes: Open Admin Roles and read what each role grants. Rename or trim until the roles match the paper plan. Open Admin Management and create each real person, then assign their roles. Sign in as one person per role and try the actions that role should and should not have. If you change a role while someone is signed in, their menus and buttons update without a reload, because the API tells their dashboard over a WebSocket. Look at the role chips on each account: they show at a glance who holds which role. Look at how permissions are grouped by module, which makes it easy to grant "view" without "edit". Before anything else, change the passwords of the sample admins under Settings, Security, or delete those accounts. The seed creates them with passwords printed in the public documentation, and the template's guides warn about this more than once for good reason. What usually goes wrong: deleting the Super Admin before another admin can manage roles, or giving the Admin role to everyone because it is easier. Start strict and loosen when someone asks. 7. Load projects and client accounts Open Projects and replace the sample rows with Larkspur's real work. A project carries a name and description in English and Arabic, a status ( in-progress , ready or blocked ), an environment, a version and an optional picture. Deleting is a soft delete: deleted projects move to their own screen and can be restored. Users work the same way. You can narrow the list by username, email, phone, name or join date, and the top of the page counts verified, unverified and deleted accounts. For Larkspur, that is the screen for client staff who got an invitation and never confirmed it. The resend-verification route answers success but sends no mail, so connect your own mail service before you rely on it. Look at the counts above the table and at the status chips on each row. If your own product has other records, the API is plain REST under /api , so you can add modules beside the existing ones. Sign in with POST /api/auth/login to get the token every other call needs, and send it as a bearer token. Lists take page and page_count , capped at 100 per page. What to check: create a project in English and Arabic, reload, and confirm both names appear when you switch language. What usually goes wrong: filling only the English name, which leaves the Arabic list with an empty label. 8. Turn on the AI assistant The assistant is its own screen. You type a question in English or Arabic and the answer is built from the dashboard's data, drawn with the same stat cards, tables, lists, donuts and charts the rest of the panel uses. It can also act: add, change, remove or bring back users, and adjust app settings. It does this only inside the permissions of the person asking. It runs on Google Gemini, OpenAI or DeepSeek, chosen in a model picker. Conversations are saved per admin in a history sidebar. You have two ways to supply a key: Put the provider's key in back-end/.env and restart the API (with Docker Compose, run docker compose up again). Then everyone with access uses your key. Leave the server without a key. The assistant then asks each person for their own, and it stays in their browser. Larkspur starts with the second option, so nobody's usage lands on the agency's bill by accident. The docs say Gemini works with free keys, while OpenAI needs billing enabled on the key. A free key can run out of quota, and the assistant says so; pick another model or wait. Control access with the ai_chat.use permission. Because the assistant can write, give it only to roles you would trust with those writes. Contractors on the Viewer role get none. Look at how the reply mixes a written summary with a chart built from the dashboard's own numbers. Two optional extras exist. A Cloudflare R2 bucket lets people upload profile pictures and image attachments; without it, uploads answer that they are not set up and everything else works. An MCP key you choose switches on the API's MCP endpoint; without one, that endpoint refuses every request. What to check: ask three questions you already know the answer to, such as how many projects are blocked, and compare. What usually goes wrong: the "asks for an API key" dialog, which only means the server has no key for the model you picked. Paste your own, or add the provider's key to the server file and restart. 9. Check Arabic and the other language details Open /ar . The page sets lang="ar" and dir="rtl" before it draws, so the sidebar moves to the right and tables and menus read right to left. The API also answers in Arabic when a request sends Accept-Language: ar , and projects, settings and countries carry both languages in the database. Anything you add should use logical Tailwind classes such as ms-2 , pe-4 , start-0 and text-start instead of ml-* , pr-* , left-* or text-left , or the Arabic page comes out wrong. If a third language is ever needed, you add its code in three locale lists, copy each en.json file under the new code, and add it to the language menu. The API keeps answering a new language in English until you add its translations in back-end/src/i18n/ . What to check: walk every screen you changed in Arabic, including the assistant. What usually goes wrong: a text added to en.json only, so the Arabic page shows a missing key. 10. Go live on a server The same docker-compose.yml that ran on the laptop also runs on a server. Give the dashboard and the API each a domain behind Caddy or Nginx, which adds HTTPS, and route the first domain to port 3030 (the dashboard) and the second to port 8000 (the API). Create .env beside docker-compose.yml and set DASHBOARD_URL and API_URL to the two public addresses. The dashboard bakes the API's address into its built code, and the API takes the same two lines for CORS_ORIGIN and FRONTEND_URL . Put your AI keys and TRUST_PROXY=1 in back-end/.env . Then start it in the background: bash docker compose up --build -d In production the API refuses to start with the example JWT_SECRET or an empty CORS_ORIGIN . With Docker it generates a secret for you and keeps it in the data volume, or you can make your own: bash node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))" When it is up, open https://api.your-domain.com/api/health (with your own domain) and look for "status":"ok" . If you prefer, the dashboard alone can go to Vercel from a private Git repository: set ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_COREPACK to 1 , then NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL , NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_BASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL . Redeploy after changing any NEXT_PUBLIC_* value, because it is compiled in at build time. Leave NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_MODE off unless the site is a public demo. The default database is SQLite, kept in the /data volume. MySQL is a configuration change: create an empty database, set DB_TYPE and the connection in back-end/.env , and seed it. Pick MySQL if your host has no persistent disk. If you run the API without Docker in production, yarn seed:prod creates the tables once; run it a single time, because a second run resets app settings and the built-in roles' permissions to their sample values. What to check: sign in from a different computer, change a role, and watch a second signed-in session update. That proves the WebSocket address is right. What usually goes wrong: empty pages with a CORS line in the browser console. The API only answers browsers from the addresses in CORS_ORIGIN , so add the dashboard's real address there and to FRONTEND_URL . Running it day to day Once Larkspur is live, the work becomes small, repeatable routines. Onboarding a person. Create the admin in Admin Management, assign one role, and send them the address. Do not share the Super Admin account. Offboarding. Delete the admin account the same day. Because roles update live, you can also strip a role from someone who is still signed in and their buttons disappear without a reload. Changing what a role may do. Edit it on the Admin Roles screen and tell the team. Test with a real account for that role. Restoring mistakes. Users and projects are soft deleted. Open the matching Deleted screen to bring one back. Backups. With SQLite in Docker, the data lives in one volume. Back that volume up on a schedule that suits how often records change. With MySQL, use your database host's backup tool. Updating. After you change code, build the images again, because a running container is a snapshot of the code at build time. Watching the assistant. Review who has ai_chat.use now and then. What it costs to run The template is a one-time purchase from $99, and the package matters: the Full Stack package that this guide uses costs more than the entry price, and the product page lists each one. The licence covers an unlimited number of projects, client work included, as long as you do not share the source code publicly. Beyond that, you pay for what you add: Hosting for the dashboard and the API. A Docker-capable server runs both; Vercel can host the dashboard alone. AI usage, if you put a provider key on the server. Google, OpenAI and DeepSeek bill by their own pricing pages. If each person brings their own key, the bill is theirs. A Cloudflare R2 bucket, if you want picture uploads, and a WeatherAPI.com key if you want the weather in the greeting. Both are optional. A domain name and, if you use it, a mail service for verification emails. What is free: local development on SQLite, the sample data, the built-in mock API in the dashboard package, and every optional feature you leave switched off. What to customise next Roles that match your company. Rename the five roles and trim their permissions until each one grants only what the job needs. Your own records. Add a module to the NestJS API for something Larkspur tracks that is not a project, such as invoices or support tickets, and a screen to match. Each domain in the API has its own module, so a new one slots in beside the others. New assistant tools. The assistant routes through an MCP registry that is built to be extended, so you can teach it questions specific to your data. A third language. Copy the message files, add the code to the three locale lists, and add the API's translations. Cleaner production code. Once your own API is the permanent source of data, the yarn remove:mock script deletes the built-in mock server, and yarn remove:demo removes the public-demo switch. Commit first, since both rewrite files. Launch checklist Sample admins deleted or their passwords changed. Your own JWT_SECRET set, or Docker's generated one confirmed in the data volume. CORS_ORIGIN and FRONTEND_URL hold the dashboard's real address. NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL points at the API with /api , and the dashboard was built after you set it. HTTPS in front of both the dashboard and the API. The health address answers "status":"ok" . Every role tested with a real account. ai_chat.use granted only where intended, and provider keys placed where you decided. Arabic checked on every screen you changed. Data volume or database backup scheduled. Demo mode off. Common mistakes Going live with the sample admins Every seed creates admins with published passwords. Change them or delete them before anyone else can reach the panel, and set your own JWT_SECRET . Editing a NEXT_PUBLIC value and expecting a change Those values are compiled into the dashboard when it is built. Rebuild (or restart yarn dev ) after any edit, and never put a secret in one: anyone can read them in the browser. Wiping data with the wrong stop command docker compose down keeps your data. Adding -v removes the volume, and everything you created goes with it. Pages stay empty and the console mentions CORS The API only answers browsers from the addresses in CORS_ORIGIN . If the dashboard runs on a new domain or port, add it there and in FRONTEND_URL . Handing the assistant to everyone The assistant can change users and settings. Grant ai_chat.use to the roles that should have that power and nobody else. Passing the example environment file to Docker The API image runs in production mode. If you start it with a copy of the example environment file, that file sets development mode over the image's own value. Pass each value you need with -e instead. FAQ How do I build an admin panel with an AI assistant in Next.js? Start from a dashboard that already has the roles, lists and chat screen, then connect your data and a model provider. In this template, the assistant reads from the same API as the rest of the panel, so you add a key and your records instead of writing chat plumbing. Do I need a backend? Only for real data. The Admin Dashboard package runs on a mock server inside the browser, which is enough for design work. For a live panel you need an API, and the Full Stack package includes a NestJS one. Which AI providers does the assistant support? Google Gemini, OpenAI and DeepSeek, picked from a model list. Each person can paste their own key, or you can set one key on the server. Does it support Arabic and RTL? Yes. Every screen, including the assistant, exists in English and Arabic, and the Arabic pages are laid out right to left. Can I use it for clients? Yes. The commercial licence covers unlimited projects, including work you build for a client and hand over. You may not publish the source code or resell it as a template. Can I change what the assistant is allowed to do? You decide who may use it through the ai_chat.use permission, and the assistant acts only within that person's own permissions. Adding new tools is done through its MCP registry in the API. Can I try it without installing anything? Yes. The live demo runs the same dashboard. For your own machine, the Admin Dashboard package runs on its built-in sample data with no API or AI key at all. Can I remove the sample data and the mock server? Yes. Two scripts, yarn remove:mock and yarn remove:demo , strip the mock server and the public-demo switch from the code. Commit first, since they rewrite files. Try it yourself Open the live demo to click through the dashboard and the assistant. The Admin Dashboard Template 2 product page lists the packages, and the documentation covers every step above in detail. More options live in the admin dashboard templates category , and the guide to admin dashboard templates by industry helps if your use case differs from this one. This template is also one of the ten in the Next.js Templates Bundle , if you expect to build more than one kind of product.

title: How to Build an Online Store with an Admin Panel in Next.js
body: Originally published on the Aniq UI blog . By the end of this guide you will know how to build an online store with an admin panel, using Next.js, NestJS and the e-commerce template from Aniq UI. You will have a storefront, an order desk for your team, and an API that holds the catalogue, customers and orders. We follow one example shop from its first plan to launch day. Each step names the screen or setting involved and uses the exact commands and file paths from the documentation. The same path works for a founder launching a store, or an agency building one for a client. About this example Cedar & Cloth is an illustrative business we use to show the steps. It is not a client story, and the numbers in it are examples, not results. The brief Cedar & Cloth is a small shop that sells linen shirts and canvas bags. The owner runs it with two people who pack orders. Here is what the shop needs: A catalogue of about thirty products, each with sizes and colors, written in English and in Arabic. Guest checkout, so a first-time visitor can buy without making an account, and track the order afterward. Payment by card, or cash on delivery for customers who prefer it. Free shipping above a set order total, and a flat fee below it. An order desk where the owner has full control and the packers can only view orders. A home page the owner can rearrange without touching code. Clean product photos on a plain background, made from phone shots. A way to see where visitors come from, using Google Analytics. How the template covers the brief Need Where it lives What you use Bilingual catalogue with variants Admin dashboard and API Products and Categories screens, with size and color variants Guest checkout and tracking Storefront The checkout page and Track Order, which asks for order number and email Card or cash on delivery Storefront and API Stripe for cards, cash on delivery selected by default Shipping rule Storefront and API A shipping config file and the orders service, kept in sync Order desk and permissions Admin dashboard Orders, Admin Management and Admin Roles Editable home page Admin dashboard The Home Page screen, section by section Product photos Admin dashboard The product form's AI studio and background removal Visitor analytics Storefront Tag ids pasted into the storefront's environment file Before you start: decisions to make A store touches money, customers and legal duties, so a few decisions are worth making before you write a line of configuration. What exactly are you selling? Count your products, and for each one decide which options a shopper chooses: size, color, or neither. Variants carry their own SKU, price adjustment and stock, so the shape of your catalogue decides how much data entry you face. Cedar & Cloth sells shirts in several sizes and colors and bags in one size. Which languages will you sell in? English and Arabic ship ready, including a right-to-left layout. Products and categories hold a name and description in both. A third language is possible for the interface, but it takes edits in several files. How will shoppers pay? Shoppers can pay by card (Stripe) or choose cash on delivery, and PayPal is not part of the checkout. Stripe charges in US dollars. If you sell in another currency, that is a decision to settle before launch, not after. What about shipping and tax? The template ships one shipping rule: free from a set order total, a flat fee below it. It applies no tax. If your business must charge tax, plan for that in code or in how you price products. Guests, accounts, or both? Both work. Guests check out with an email and track orders by number and email. Customers with accounts also get saved addresses, order history and a wishlist. Who handles email? The template sends none: no confirmations, no shipping notices, no password resets. Choose a mail provider early, because customers expect at least an order confirmation. Which AI tools, if any? Each one needs its own key, and some need the media bucket. Decide which are worth turning on for launch. A shop that only needs clean product photos can enable background removal and nothing else. Step by step Step 1: Choose the package The template has four packages: Full Stack (storefront, admin and API), Storefront alone, Admin Dashboard alone, and Backend API alone. The two frontends can each run by themselves on a built-in sample store inside the browser. That is useful for a design pass, but real orders, payments and AI features need the NestJS API. Cedar & Cloth takes the Full Stack package. The commercial license covers unlimited projects, including stores you build and hand over to a client. The My templates page lists a ZIP for each package, so choose the one you bought. What to check: the Full Stack ZIP extracts to e-commerce-1 , containing admin-dashboard , back-end , storefront and docker-compose.yml . Single-app packages extract to their own folder with a Dockerfile , package.json and .env.example . Step 2: Run it locally with Docker Download the ZIP from My templates, unzip it, and open a terminal in the e-commerce-1 folder. Start Docker, then run: docker compose up --build Docker builds three images on the first run and loads a demo store into the database, so expect a few minutes. The storefront opens at localhost:3030 , the admin at localhost:3031 , and the API at localhost:8000 . A busy port can be moved with SITE_PORT , ADMIN_PORT or API_PORT in a .env file next to docker-compose.yml . Sign in to the admin as the Super Admin ( admin@example.com , password Admin@123 ) and to the storefront as a demo customer ( john.doe@example.com , password password123 ). A read-only staff account, john.smith@admin.com with admin123 , shows what the Viewer role sees. Place a test order as the customer, then find it in the admin. One honest note: on the admin overview, several cards (revenue, sales, goal, visitors, conversion and the map) display placeholder figures until you connect your own numbers. Check which cards are wired to real data before you rely on them. This still shows a terminal opened inside the extracted folder, which is where each command should run. Look for the API passing its health check, since the two frontends start only after it does. The Node.js route starts with the API, after the seed has created the database and demo store. The admin dashboard runs in its own terminal on port 3031, beside the storefront on 3030. The screenshot above is the admin overview you should see after signing in as the Super Admin. What to check: open localhost:8000/api/health , which should answer with a status of ok. Then add a product to the cart as the demo customer, check out as a guest, and find the order in the admin. What usually goes wrong: Docker is not running, or port 3030, 3031 or 8000 is taken. Free it, or set SITE_PORT , ADMIN_PORT or API_PORT to a free number. The first start seems stuck. It is seeding the demo store, and the frontends start only when the API is healthy. A "Sample data" notice shows. The frontend was built without an API address and is running on its own sample store. Yarn reports version 1.22. Run corepack enable and install again. Step 3: Make it Cedar & Cloth The brand lives in files, and the storefront and the admin keep their own copies. In the storefront, src/config/brand.config.ts holds the store name (it ships as a text wordmark), the browser tab name, the contact details and the social links, each with English and Arabic values. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL to your real domain, because canonical links, the sitemap and sharing cards use it. The shipped copy describes a menswear shop. Three places carry that copy: the text blocks in brand.config.ts , the messages/home/ folder for the home page, and messages/seo/ for page titles. Cedar & Cloth sells menswear too, so it edits less than most shops will. Each app keeps its colors in src/styles/theme-variables.css , as CSS variables, with a block for light and a block for dark. The accent is --primaryColor . The storefront loads Plus Jakarta Sans for Latin text and two Arabic fonts. The admin has its own brand file and uses the system font stack. What to check: rebuild, then look for the old name in the browser tab, the footer, the sharing preview and the Arabic pages. Replace the placeholder contact details, since they ship as placeholders. What usually goes wrong: the footer shows no social icons, because the links ship empty and only filled ones appear. Another is a sharing image that still shows the template's hero photo. Point meta.ogImage at your own picture. Step 4: Add categories and products Start with categories: a name and description in both languages, plus an image, a slug, a sort position and an on/off switch. They are one flat level. Then add products. A product takes: A name and descriptions in both languages (only the English name is mandatory), a slug, a SKU and a category. A price, an optional compare-at price, a cost price and a stock count. Up to 12 images and videos in any order, one marked primary, each with alt text. Variants such as Size with M, or Colour with its hex code. Each variant has its own SKU, price adjustment and stock. Flags for active, featured and best seller, and free tags. Uploads go to a Cloudflare R2 bucket, or another S3-compatible store, and fail with a 503 until you fill in the five R2_* variables in back-end/.env . The demo catalogue itself renders from bundled files, so you can build the whole flow before you set a bucket. Work in this order, so nothing points at something that does not exist yet: Create categories first, since every product needs one. Add one complete product, with photos, variants and both languages, before you add the rest. Open it on the storefront in English and Arabic and check the gallery, the variant picker and the price. Only then repeat for the remaining products. Look at the flat list of categories with their order and active switch: the sort order here shapes the categories row on the home page. The compact view fits more rows on screen, which helps when you are checking stock and prices across many products. What to check: deleted products have their own list, so check where one lands after you remove it. Variant SKUs must be unique, so use a clear naming pattern from the start. What usually goes wrong: uploads fail with a 503, because the bucket variables are not set. Or images load at full size, because the frontends were not told your bucket's public host. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_MEDIA_HOSTNAME to that host, without https:// , and rebuild. Step 5: Arrange the home page The Home Page screen in the admin decides, one section at a time, what shoppers see on the storefront's front page. Categories need only an order. The other sections take a capped number of products or texts: up to 3 style pillars, 2 editorial panels, 6 new drops, 8 best sellers, 6 spotlight items and 5 slides in the closing slider. If New drops is empty, it shows the newest products. Editing a section needs the products.edit permission. What to check: add a product that uses every section, then open the storefront home page and confirm each section shows what you picked. Empty the New drops section and confirm it falls back to the newest products. What usually goes wrong: a change does not appear because you lack the products.edit permission, or because the storefront is on its sample store and not reading the API. Step 6: Set shipping, payments and the order flow The checkout offers card through Stripe, and cash on delivery. Cash on delivery is selected by default, and the API always prices an order from its own catalogue, never from numbers the browser sends. There is no PayPal option. The shipping rule ships as free from $75 and $9.99 below that, with no tax. It is written in two places, storefront/src/config/shipping.ts and back-end/src/modules/orders/orders.service.ts . Edit both in one change, or the cart and the charge will disagree. To take cards, use Stripe test keys first: Add both STRIPE_SECRET_KEY and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET to back-end/.env . Put NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY in the storefront's .env and rebuild. In the Stripe dashboard, create a webhook endpoint that points to your API address plus /api/payments/webhook , and have it listen for two events: payment_intent.succeeded and payment_intent.payment_failed . A card order stays pending until Stripe calls that webhook, then becomes paid and confirmed. For local testing, the Stripe CLI can relay events to http://localhost:8000/api/payments/webhook . In the admin, an order moves one step at a time: pending, confirmed, processing, shipped, delivered, or cancelled before it closes. Add the tracking number when you ship, and download any order as a CSV file. What to check: place a cash on delivery order and a card order with Stripe test keys. The first should be confirmed and unpaid. The second should be pending until the webhook arrives, then paid and confirmed. Fail a card on purpose and confirm the order is marked failed. What usually goes wrong: The card option is missing at checkout. The publishable key is empty or not a real test or live key, which leaves cash on delivery as the only choice. Card orders stay pending. The webhook endpoint or its signing secret is wrong. The storefront still shows the old publishable key. It is compiled in, so rebuild after changing it. Step 7: Add staff and set their permissions Staff accounts live under Admin Management, and their permissions under Admin Roles. The seed gives you a Super Admin with every permission and a Viewer role with every view permission, which leaves out the AI assistant. The Admin, Manager and Editor roles exist but start with nothing, so tick their permissions before you give them to anyone. Cedar & Cloth keeps the owner as Super Admin. For the two packers it gives view access to orders, plus the edit permission that moving an order forward requires. Everything else stays hidden from them, because the sidebar and the API check the same permission names. What to check: sign in as the Viewer account and confirm it can see lists but not change them. Then sign in as the packer role you created and confirm moving an order forward works. What usually goes wrong: a new staff member sees almost nothing, because their role has no permissions ticked. Permission changes reach signed-in staff over a live connection, so they do not need to sign out. Step 8: Add the AI tools you want Each AI feature switches on only when its key is in back-end/.env , and a key still holding its example value counts as unset. Admin assistant: needs a Google Gemini key. It answers questions about the shop, finds orders, edits products and stock, and draws sales charts, all within the signed-in admin's permissions. AI product studio: in the product form. Its assistant mode needs a Gemini key and the media bucket. Its Animate mode needs a Higgsfield key and secret. Fitting room: lets shoppers see a product worn on a model or on their own photo. It needs a Gemini key and the bucket. Background removal: needs a model file on your own server and the bucket, but no key, and it costs nothing per image. Cedar & Cloth turns on only background removal, so the phone shots become clean catalogue photos. The Docker image leaves the model out unless you ask for it when you build. Provider charges for the keyed features are yours. What to check: open the AI Assistant page and ask for a sales summary. Confirm the answer comes with a chart drawn from your own data. For background removal, open a product photo and confirm the Remove background button appears. What usually goes wrong: a feature reports itself off. Either its key is missing or still holds the example value, or it needs the media bucket as well. The studio, the fitting room and background removal all need the bucket. Also remember that the assistant and the studio are unavailable on the sample store. Step 9: Wire up analytics Six ad and analytics networks are built into the storefront. Paste an id into storefront/.env and rebuild. A blank id loads no script. The variables are NEXT_PUBLIC_GTM_ID , NEXT_PUBLIC_GA4_MEASUREMENT_ID , NEXT_PUBLIC_META_PIXEL_ID , NEXT_PUBLIC_TIKTOK_PIXEL_ID , NEXT_PUBLIC_SNAPCHAT_PIXEL_ID and NEXT_PUBLIC_PINTEREST_TAG_ID . If you set only one, make it Google Tag Manager, which can load the others itself. If GA4 already runs inside your Tag Manager container, leave the GA4 variable blank, or every session counts twice. The storefront reports page views, product views, add to cart, begin checkout, purchase, search and sign-up. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_DEBUG=true to log each event in the browser console while testing. The tags load as soon as a page does. If you sell to the EU or the UK, show a consent banner before they run. What to check: turn on debug logging, click through a purchase and watch the events appear in the browser console in order: product view, add to cart, begin checkout, purchase. Then confirm the same events in Tag Manager's preview or your analytics tool. What usually goes wrong: a change to an id has no effect, since ids are compiled in and need a rebuild. Or the purchase event fires without the right currency. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_CURRENCY if you do not sell in US dollars. Step 10: Go live Fix the gaps the template leaves open, then deploy: It sends no email at all: no order confirmation, no shipping notice, no password reset. Connect a mail provider in the forgotPassword hook of back-end/src/modules/customer-auth/customer-auth.controller.ts and for orders. Both the contact form and the newsletter signup acknowledge the visitor yet deliver nothing, and no terms or privacy pages come with the template. Connect the forms and write the pages. Then configure the API in back-end/.env : a fresh JWT_SECRET (made with node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))" ), NODE_ENV=production , CORS_ORIGIN listing the storefront and admin addresses, and FRONTEND_URL set to the admin's address. Build the API, run yarn db:sync:prod once to create the tables, and start it. In each frontend set NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL with /api on the end and rebuild. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_STOREFRONT_URL in the admin so its Go to storefront link works. Do not use yarn railway:setup for a live shop: it drops every table each time it runs. Change the published demo passwords, or start from empty tables. What to check after going live: place a real small order on your domain, watch it appear in the admin with a notification, move it through its statuses, and track it as a guest with the order number and email. Confirm the notification bell is live, which means the admin's address matches FRONTEND_URL . What usually goes wrong: Browsers are blocked by the API. CORS_ORIGIN must list both frontends exactly as the browser shows them. Everyone gets "Too many attempts" behind a proxy. Each of those routes (sign-in, registration, password reset, guest tracking) accepts ten requests a minute from one address. Set TRUST_PROXY to how many proxies stand in front. Password reset goes nowhere. In production the reset token is not delivered until you connect a mail provider. Running it day to day When the shop is live, the owner and packers use a short list of admin screens. Starting the day on the overview The overview sits at the top of the sidebar and shows the shop at a glance. Remember that several cards display placeholder figures until you connect real numbers, so keep a separate, trusted source for revenue until you do. Look at the latest orders and the bell in the top bar, which is where new activity shows first. Moving orders along Filter the list by order status or payment status; the newest orders come first. Open an order, check the items, totals and addresses, add the tracking number when it ships, and move it forward one step. Cancel only before the order is closed. The payment status is set by the payment, never by hand. The fulfilment progress on each row shows how far an order has moved, so packers can scan for what is still waiting. Helping a customer The customers screen lists the shop's customers, and deleted ones have their own list. A customer who cannot track an order needs the exact order number and the email used at checkout, because tracking asks for both. Use this list to find a customer by account and open their record when they write to you. Keeping the storefront fresh Rearrange the home page sections when you launch a new product, add an offer, or want a best seller pushed forward. Those edits are made in the admin, so they need no code change. Settings are stored values The App settings tab holds key and value pairs, including payment, email and general ones. The shipped storefront and API do not read them yet, so changing one changes nothing until your own code does. An example launch plan by week This schedule is an example for Cedar & Cloth, not a promise about how long your launch will take. Week 1, understand. Run the stack, place a test order, and settle the decisions list. Week 2, brand and catalogue. Rebrand both apps, rewrite the shipped copy, and add categories and one complete product. Week 3, the rest of the shop. Add the remaining products, arrange the home page, and set up bucket storage and photos. Week 4, money and staff. Set the shipping rule, connect Stripe in test mode, create the roles for the packers, and run orders through every status. Week 5, production. Set up hosting, the environment files and the tables. Connect a mail provider, add tracking tags, and write the missing terms and privacy pages. Week 6, soft launch. Start with a small audience, then switch to Stripe live keys when you are sure. Launch checklist Store name, logos, icons, colors and fonts replaced in both apps. Shipped menswear copy rewritten in the brand file, the home messages and the SEO messages. Contact details, social links and sharing images replaced. Categories and products complete in both languages, with variants and photos. Shipping rule changed in both files, if you changed it at all. Stripe live keys and the live webhook in place, after a full test-mode run. Roles ticked for each staff member, and the demo passwords changed. JWT_SECRET , CORS_ORIGIN , FRONTEND_URL and both frontend API addresses set for production. NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL set to the real domain. A mail provider connected, and the contact form and newsletter form wired. Terms and privacy pages written. Tracking ids pasted, and a consent banner added if you sell to the EU or UK. Demo checkout prefill left off. Backups scheduled for the database and the media bucket. Template, from scratch, or a hosted store builder A hosted store builder You can be selling quickly, with hosting, checkout and updates handled for you. You pay ongoing fees, work within the platform's design and rules, and keep your data on their system. It suits a shop that wants to sell, not to run software. Building from scratch You get exactly what you design. You also build a catalogue with variants, carts, guest checkout, order tracking, payment and webhooks, accounts for customers and staff, permissions, an admin, two languages and an API before the first order. You maintain all of it. Starting from a template You own the code, host the stack and change anything. The storefront, admin and API are already connected, so you spend your time on products and brand. In return you accept the work this guide lists: email, tax rules, terms pages, hosting and updates. It suits founders who want control, and agencies building stores for clients. What it costs to run Template packages start from $79, and the Full Stack package Cedar & Cloth uses is $179. It includes a commercial license and lifetime support. Beyond that you pay for what you switch on: Hosting for the storefront, admin and API, and a database if you move past SQLite. Stripe's processing fees, listed on Stripe's pricing page . Cash on delivery needs no processor. A bucket such as Cloudflare R2 for product images. A Google Gemini key for the assistant, studio or fitting room, billed by Google, and a Higgsfield account for video. A mail provider and a domain. Free parts: SQLite for local work, the demo store, cash on delivery, and background removal on your own server. What to customise next Copy and photos. Replace the home page messages and the page titles in both languages. Shipping rules. Change the free-shipping threshold or fee in the two files together. Another tracking network. The marketing tags are configured in src/config/analytics.config.ts , and the template describes adding one more as a single-file job. Admin overview cards. Wire the sample revenue and conversion cards to your own numbers. Roles. Build a role for each person on the team. A third language. Add it to both frontends and the API. Products hold two languages, English and Arabic. Common mistakes Card orders that stay pending An order flips to paid only after Stripe's webhook reaches your API; the shopper coming back to the site does not do it. Check the endpoint address, the two subscribed events and the signing secret. Changing the shipping rule in only one place The cart, checkout summary and API must agree. Edit the storefront config and the orders service in the same change. Leaving the frontends on the sample store Without NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL , each frontend answers from sample data in the browser, shows a notice, and charges no one. Set the address and rebuild. Counting every GA4 session twice If GA4 loads from Tag Manager, leave the template's GA4 variable empty. Handing out an empty role Admin, Manager and Editor start with no permissions. A staff member given one sees almost nothing until you tick what they need. FAQ How do I build an online store with an admin panel in Next.js? Use a template that already has the storefront, the dashboard and the API as one project, and change the brand and catalogue. This one gives you all three, with a seeder that fills the database with a demo store in one command. Can I use it for clients? Yes. The license covers unlimited projects, including stores built for a customer and handed over. You may not resell the code or release it as a template. Does it support Arabic and RTL? Yes. The storefront, the admin and the API ship in English and Arabic, with Arabic laid out right to left. Products and categories are stored with both languages. Do I need a backend? For real orders, yes. The frontends run alone on a sample store, but real orders, payments and AI features depend on the NestJS API, which comes with the Full Stack and Backend API packages. Does it support guest checkout? Yes. Guests check out with an email and track the order by number and email, with no account. Which payment methods work? Card payments run on Stripe, and shoppers can also choose cash on delivery. PayPal is not offered at checkout. Which database does it use? SQLite for local work and MySQL by configuration, with no code change. Does it handle tax? No. The shipping rule and checkout total apply no tax. If your business must charge it, add that to the pricing logic on both the storefront and the API so the totals stay equal. Can customers pay in other currencies? Card payments are charged in US dollars. Selling in another currency means changing that in code, and the tracking currency is a separate setting. What happens when a card is declined? The order is marked failed when Stripe reports the failed payment. Cash on delivery remains available for that customer. Try it yourself Open the storefront demo and the admin demo . Then read the documentation or visit the e-commerce template page . More choices are in the e-commerce templates category and the Next.js e-commerce templates guide . The e-commerce template is also one of the ten templates in the Next.js Templates Bundle .

title: 5 things that broke while building paid Discord & Telegram access with Stripe and Supabase
body: I'm building Kordhub , a tool that lets creators sell access to their Discord server or Telegram group. Someone pays with Stripe, the bot gives them a role. They cancel, the role is removed. Sounds simple. Here are 5 things that broke while testing it with real payments. 1. Stripe sends the same cancellation twice When a member cancels from the Stripe customer portal, Stripe fires two customer.subscription.updated events almost at the same time (the second one carries the cancellation survey answer). Both read the old state before either wrote, so I logged the cancellation twice. Fix: make the update conditional ("only if it's not already canceling") and ask for the updated rows back. If nothing comes back, another event already handled it, so skip the log and the notification. 2. The bot can't assign a role above its own Discord returns 403 (code 50013) if the bot's role is below the role you're trying to give. New servers hit this all the time, because the bot's role lands at the bottom when it joins. Fix: catch that exact code and tell the creator in plain words: "drag the Kordhub role above the role you're selling, then tap Re-send access". Turning a cryptic error into one instruction saved a support ticket. 3. Telegram won't remove the group owner When a subscription expired, my Telegram ban call failed with Bad Request: can't remove chat owner . I was testing with my own account, which owns the group. Lesson: owners and admins can't be removed by a bot. Treat that error as "nothing to do", not as something to retry forever. 4. Don't DM people directly from your webhook Discord rate limits are global per bot. Sending DMs straight from the payment webhook works in testing and falls over with real traffic. Fix: every DM goes into a queue (a Postgres table + a small worker), so a burst of sales never fights the rate limit and failures are logged per job. 5. Expiration needs its own clock Stripe tells you when a subscription is deleted, but not every access type has a Stripe subscription (one-time passes, manual grants). A scheduled job (pg_cron every 5 minutes) checks expires_at , removes access, and cancels anything still open in Stripe. Stack Supabase (Postgres, Auth, Edge Functions, pg_cron), Stripe Connect with direct charges, Cloudflare Pages, vanilla JS. If you're building something similar, I hope this saves you a few hours. And if you run a paid community, you can try it free at kordhub.com .

title: Workers AI and AI Gateway: using AI on Cloudflare without scattering API keys
body:
If you run several small projects, API keys tend to pile up: one per provider, copied into env files, CI secrets and old branches. Every copy is one more place a key can leak.
One way out is to keep inference inside Cloudflare. Workers AI runs models from a Worker binding, so there's no external key in the code at all, and AI Gateway sits in front of external providers so the provider key lives in one place, with caching, rate limits and logs on top.
I wrote up how I set this up across my projects, with the trade-offs I hit along the way (in Portuguese): https://kevinbk.com/blog/evitar-acumulo-de-chaves-api-em-projetos-ia

title: AI League-Coach
body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built League Coach is a stats-driven coach for League of Legends. You give it match stats (CS, deaths, vision, KDA, win/loss per game). It compares them to role benchmarks, finds your biggest gaps, and a local LLM turns them into a short coaching plan: your biggest problem, three drills for your next five games, and one thing you do well. Who would pay: ranked grinders stuck in a rank who can't afford human coaching ($20-50/hour), and small coaches or Discord communities who want to triage students' stats before a session. Possible pricing: a free CLI, then a paid hosted version with Riot API auto-import and a weekly progress report. Demo sarvesh-amb.github.io Code Sarvesh-Amb / league-coach this is completely ai generated, I just wanted the sticker I am sorry :( it's supposed to be a league coach, at least I hope it works well View on GitHub How I Built It Rules engine (pure Python, stdlib only): groups games by role and computes CS/min, vision/min, deaths in wins vs losses, and KDA. It ranks gaps against editable role benchmarks. The numbers come from code, not the model, so the LLM can't make up your stats. Open-weight LLM via Ollama: the flagged gaps go to a local model (Llama 3.1 8B by default; Qwen 2.5 and others work via --model ), which writes the coaching under a strict "use only these numbers" system prompt. Graceful fallback: if no model is running, you still get the rules-based findings. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? A coach is only useful if you run it after every session, so cost per run matters. With open weights it's free to run locally with no API key or rate limits. Your match history stays on your machine. And anyone can swap in a better model or edit the benchmarks for their own role, patch, or game, which a closed API wouldn't let me promise users.

title: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’
body:
Anthropic announced on Sunday that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good.
Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.”
There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study . But, the company said, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.”
If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

title: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink
body:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine .
U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations.
In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed.
Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims.
"President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press."
"President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added.
Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX , is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield .
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal.
Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said.
Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA . Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high.
Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"
Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress.
"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X . "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."

Mister Organ doesn’t reach the level of societal horror of The Act of Killing or the creepypasta-meets-true-crime gruesomeness of Beware the Slenderman , but there’s something deeply unsettling about Michael Organ and his intimate campaign of terror against everyone who enters his life.
Mister Organ is a documentary by David Farrier, an Auckland, New Zealand journalist. The movie starts with Farrier reporting on Bashford Antiques, a shop in Ponsonby that has begun aggressively clamping cars in its lot and demanding exorbitant fees to release them — up to $760. Farrier’s article for The Spinoff eventually led the government to introduce legislation that would outlaw extreme clamping fees .
Under normal circumstances, that would be the end of the story. But at the center of this story is a man named Michael Organ who turns out to be a bizarre, seemingly dangerous conman.
Organ was hired to police Bashford’s lot, and during his investigation, Farrier discovers he’s more than just a parking-lot bully. Years earlier, Organ had been charged with attempting to steal a yacht in an elaborate scheme. What’s more, he claimed to be a prince and a lawyer — he is neither.
As Farrier talks to people who have known Organ and interacts with him directly, what emerges is a portrait of a deeply troubled man who has left a trail of traumatized people in his wake. The movie shifts from a wild portrait of a conman to something more alarming and tense when Organ reveals he’s gotten his hands on a key to Farrier’s home and only warns him to be careful.
From there it spirals even further; eventually, Farrier felt it necessary to leave the country to protect himself from Organ’s campaign of harassment and gaslighting. It’s the rare documentary that doubles as a psychological horror film.

title: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
body:
“You Can See Everything” is already a box office sensation, with a $15 million opening weekend (based on Sunday estimates). That’s the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
The nearly three-hour movie — first revealed last month at a secretive screening at the Telluride Film Festival — is only playing in 855 theaters this weekend. (In contrast, the weekend’s No. 1 movie, “Street Fighter,” is playing in 3,575.) But it had a reported 2,000 sellout screenings, and the reviews are overwhelmingly positive: “You Can See Everything” currently has a score of 99% on both Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic .
The story of Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall — founding blood-testing startup Theranos, attracting support from many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, then ultimately being sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors — has already been told in books, podcasts, TV shows, and other documentaries.
But the documentary’s filmmakers were given extensive access to Holmes and her family in the month before she went to jail, and the involvement of “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder — who co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim — made the whole thing even more intriguing.
While I haven’t seen the movie, I can at least attest to the difficulty of finding tickets in Manhattan: I spent a good chunk of yesterday trying to find a screening for tonight, and I found exactly one with seats available that weren’t in the front row. (Yes, of course I’m going.)
TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling already got to see it on Thursday . She wrote that the enigmatic Holmes finally seems to have met her match in Fielder, a deadpan comedian who’s arguably just as strange and mysterious as she is. Fielder’s month with Holmes is apparently just the beginning of what sounds like an increasingly surreal, metatextual odyssey.
The discussion around “You Can See Everything” may be making it harder for other tech-centric films to break through. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Network” follow-up “The Social Reckoning” opened to a disappointing $5.5 million last weekend and has already fallen entirely out of the top 10. And Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” — hampered, perhaps, by resistance from social platforms and a four-hour runtime — made only $306,702 this weekend.

title: The Nuclear Power Shortcut That Could Add Gigawatts to the U.S. Grid
body: The process of increasing the maximum power level at which a commercial nuclear power plant may operate is called a power uprate. Several nuclear plants are now considering applying for permission to uprate operations to produce more power in the mid-term to bridge the gap while more nuclear capacity is being developed.  The United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission NRC regulates the maximum power level at which a commercial nuclear power plant may operate. The permitted power level is stated in the license and technical specifications for the plant and cannot be altered unless approved by the NRC. U.S. nuclear plants can request permission from the NRC to increase their power output, or "uprate".  The NRC will determine whether to grant a plant uprate permission depending on whether it can be achieved safely. To increase power output, nuclear operators must modify the nuclear reactor's instrumentation, controls, and power-generation systems. Over the past two decades, the NRC has approved uprates that have provided an extra 6 GW of power to the U.S. electricity grid, which is equivalent to six large reactors. The agency is considering uprate requests from various operators that massively boost the country's nuclear power capacity.  To safely uprate operations, plant operators must upgrade components such as controls, turbines, and pumps within their nuclear facilities to generate more electricity. While these upgrades can cost billions of dollars to implement, they can allow operators to produce more power much more quickly than it takes to build a new facility. Many upgrades can be completed in five years or less. Analysts estimated that increasing electricity output from existing nuclear plants could add a massive 6-8 GW of clean power to the grid.  In October, the largest nuclear power plant operator in the United States, Constellation Energy, announced plans to invest over $4.3 billion to refurbish 11 reactors at six plants in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey, enabling them to produce more power. The investment is expected to help Constellation add 890 MW of power to the grid, enough to supply 700,000 homes. Google has agreed to buy electricity from those plants at an undisclosed price.  This is just one of several projects that are expected to support the massive increase in U.S. power demand driven by the rapid rollout of new artificial intelligence AI data centres. Also this month, the U.S. Department of Energy DoE announced it would conditionally loan the energy company Vistra $4.2 billion to uprate three nuclear plants in Pennsylvania and Ohio, adding another 430 MW of capacity. Amazon also completed an agreement to uprate Constellation's Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant in Maryland, while Google announced plans to increase power production from four reactors in Georgia.  The Trump administration, which has announced plans to quadruple the U.S. nuclear power capacity by 2050, is highly supportive of these new projects. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement, "By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, around-the-clock energy."  Several nuclear plant operators have struggled to secure the funds to upgrade their plants as U.S. power demand plateaued in the 2000s and public perception of nuclear power was poor. However, the rising demand for power driven by data centres and the improved public perception of nuclear power has encouraged tech companies to invest heavily in a wide range of energy projects, from nuclear power to gas plants and renewable sources. Several tech companies are now willing to pump vast amounts of capital into uprating projects to rapidly increase their access to the clean power needed to run massive data centres.  The NRC expects a total of 31 power uprate applications totalling 7.3 GW thermal and 2.4 GW electric between 2026 and 2032. The organisation is expected to approve several of these projects, as many of the operators requesting uprate permissions have decades of experience in nuclear power development in the United States, making them well-versed in managing safety concerns.  Some operators are wary of conducting uprate work because the necessary upgrades would require them to stop producing power for several months. However, as tech companies demonstrate their willingness to invest heavily in nuclear energy projects, more companies may be convinced in the coming years.  Uprating operations is unlikely to detract from plans to develop new nuclear plants in the United States, given the projected rise in power demand over the coming decades. However, it could provide an alternative way to rapidly expand the country's nuclear power capacity to fill the gap while new facilities are being designed, licensed, and constructed.  By Felicity Bradstock for Oilprice.com

title: Florida's HOAs and condo associations are making the housing crisis worse
body:
A housing crisis has three parts: what a home costs, how many are for sale, and whether the people in them get to stay. In Florida the homeowner and condominium associations push on all three. HOA Spy indexes 104,659 Florida associations â the 27,377 with a unit count on file hold 1,518,436 homes between them. Their records show 10,296 foreclosure suits the associations brought against their own members, 460,412 claims of lien and 277,047 lis pendens recorded against homes, 48,999 court records in all, and 6,661 associations whose own corporation has lapsed or fallen out of standing. Every count on this page comes from official court dockets and county records, and every community named links to its own record; the dues and price figures are someone else's, dated and linked where they appear. Suits and liens are counts of filings, not of homes lost.
8,148 of the 13,601 Florida communities with court records (rings â red where foreclosure is the most common case type) and 8,165 of the 34,198 with recorded liens (dots, coloured by liens in the last five years) have an address or ZIP in the record and are drawn here. Click a pin for the community's report, or open the full-screen map .
An association exists to keep a community maintained and insured and to collect the dues that pay for it. The records show what else the 104,659 Florida associations do with the powers the law gives them, and what it does to the housing around them.
Florida law gives every association a lien on each home for unpaid assessments and the right to foreclose it â section 720.3085, Florida Statutes for homeowners' associations, section 718.116, Florida Statutes for condominiums. The debt that starts it can be a few hundred dollars; by the time a suit is filed it carries interest, late charges, collection costs and the association's attorney's fees, all secured by the lien. 10,296 foreclosure suits on file were brought by a Florida association against one of its own members, from 2,695 communities â 2.6% of those indexed. The lender's foreclosures that merely name an association number 1,629: the association is the foreclosing party more often than the bank is.
The peak was 2009, with 875 suits (about 2 a day); 2025, the last full year, had 599, and 667 have been filed so far in 2026.
Each suit is a household that may be forced to sell, a home that may go to auction for the debt and the fees, and a sale that takes place under a deadline instead of on the market. A foreclosure suit is not a lost home â most end when the owner, or the owner's lender, pays â but the pressure is the point.
