Before any suit there is a claim of lien, a one-page document in the county's official records against the home. A lien does not have to be foreclosed to do damage: a title company will not close a sale over it, a lender will not refinance behind it, and clearing it means paying whatever the association's lawyer says is owed. In the recorder indexes HOA Spy collects (Broward County Official Records index, Miami-Dade County Official Records index), 460,412 claims of lien have been recorded by associations since 1978, and 277,047 lis pendens â 60% of the liens were followed by a foreclosure filing. 5,702 communities recorded a lien in the last five years; 1,047 liens on file were contested.
2025 saw 7,916 claims of lien, up 8% on 2020 (7,352); the peak was 2008 with 29,518.
claims of lien lis pendens Â· 2026 is partial
The communities with the most liens on record: BEACHPLACE TOWERS CONDOMINIUM ASSOCIATION, INC. (8,798); PALM-AIRE RESORT OWNERS ASSN (4,951); SILVERLAKES COMMUNITY ASSOCIATION, INC. (4,569); BEACH PLACE TOWERS CONDO ASSN INC (2,602); CHAPEL TRAIL OWNERS ASSN INC (2,407).
Since the Surfside collapse, Senate Bill 4-D (2022) and the laws that followed it require older condominium buildings to pass a milestone structural inspection (section 553.899, Florida Statutes) and to fund structural reserves on the strength of a structural integrity reserve study (section 718.112(2)(g), Florida Statutes), reserves the owners can no longer vote to waive. The repairs and the reserves are paid by the owners, through higher dues and special assessments, and an owner who cannot pay is back at step one above.
The cost is visible in the dues. Redfin reported in August 2024 that median monthly HOA fees in the three months to July 2024, against a year earlier, rose Tampa 17.2% to $614 a month, Orlando 16.7% to $467 a month, Fort Lauderdale 16.2% to $611 a month, against 5.7% across the metros it tracked ( Redfin ).
Buyers price that in: Mortgage Professional America reported in January 2026, citing housing analyst Nick Gerli, that condo values in Florida fell 9.9% over the preceding twelve months ( source ). A home that costs more each month to keep and less to sell is the crisis in one sentence.
No public index records what an association charges, so HOA Spy cannot count the assessments. What it can count is what happens when they go unpaid â the liens and foreclosure suits above.
Every suit an association files or defends is paid for out of the dues â and the cost of a suit an owner wins is still passed back to the owners. 48,999 court records name a Florida association, from 13,601 communities. The association is the plaintiff in 29,947 of them and the defendant in 14,113; when it is sued, the most common suit is Appellate (4,380). 92 communities have fifty or more cases each â litigation as a matter of routine. The ten busiest communities account for 2% of all the records. Among the 24,664 closed cases with both dates on the docket, half took more than 223 days.
An association is a corporation, and a corporation that is dissolved, delinquent or not in good standing with the state cannot reliably insure the property, keep its reserves, sign a contract or answer a lender's questionnaire â which is enough to stall every sale in the community. Of the 104,659 Florida associations checked against the state's corporate registry, 3,753 have no active corporation on file and 2,908 are delinquent in their registration â 6% in all.
Corporate status as the registry records it: active (51,981).
The county is the community's own, from its registration or ZIP. Court records are counted only in the courts HOA Spy indexes and liens only in the recorder indexes it collects, so a county whose portal is not read shows few or none.
Florida associations bring more foreclosure suits against their members than those of any other state on HOA Spy. 10,296 of the 14,168 on file (73%); Texas is next with 2,349.
These are counts of records on file, not rates. Florida has 104,659 indexed associations â more than any other state â and its county courts publish deep case histories, so it counts more. Per hundred communities, Florida has 47 court records; Maryland has 603 and Texas has 231. A state whose courts hide older cases ranks lower whatever its associations do.
Foreclosure cases are the dockets whose nature of suit is a foreclosure, in the courts HOA Spy indexes; the association's side is the role the court recorded, else the caption. title: Second Chinese Submarine Drone Mothership Emerges
body: Nearly a month ago, we reported on a uniquely configured vessel that was far along in its construction at Hudong-Zhonghua Shipyard on Changxing Island in Shanghai. The intentions behind this design appeared to be as an uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) mothership, capable of deploying a handful of very large vehicles or many more smaller ones via its stern garage door and well deck. Its large pylons would be used to lift the vessels up and down out of the water and to different levels in the ship. Now it appears China has not just one, but two of these vessels nearly complete. Make sure to read our initial report on this vessel configuration for full context by clicking here . (Chinese Internet) The new image was taken in Guangzhou and the vessel has a near identical shape, but with smaller proportions and minor changes to its overall moldline, compared to the larger one in Shanghai. This new vessel appears to be about a third smaller overall than its counterpart. The lift towers number six in total instead of six larger ones and six smaller ones on the Shanghai vessel. Regardless, the major design features are all there, including the flight deck and hangar behind the forward superstructure, the location of the smokestacks, and so on. The larger but very similar in configuration UUV mothership that has now been launched in Shanghai. (Chinese Internet) While two of these assets could still be considered largely intended for experimental use, a growing fleet would have increasing tactical and even strategic importance. Being able to easily launch and recover large numbers of UUVs, or a few very large ones, far from Chinese shores would provide an asymmetric capability. A fleet of ships that is dedicated to deploying, recovering, and tending to these systems, some of which can remain on patrol for very long periods, would be a major indication of how important China sees UUV operations as part of its future strategy. 03 September 2025, China, Beijing: HSU100 uncrewed underwater drones ride along on military transporters at Tiananmen Square in Beijing during a military parade to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. Photo: Johannes Neudecker/dpa (Photo by Johannes Neudecker/picture alliance via Getty Images) picture alliance There have been rumors that these vessels are part of a larger overall program that will see more ships with similar capabilities constructed. Once again, this would be a strong indication that these vessels’ utility will go beyond testing and limited operational use cases. The launch and recovery of large UUVs remains a conceptual work in progress for the U.S., with nothing similar in the U.S. Navy’s inventory, as we discussed in our original post . Large long-range UUVs can be used for many tasks, from mapping the sea floor to hunting submarines and ships to searching for mines to launching cruise missiles and drones to being turned into immensely destructive weapons in their own right that can circumvent traditional strategic defenses. For China, providing a credible threat to America’s outposts deep in the Pacific and even the U.S. seaboard would be on the table. An AJX002 uncrewed underwater vehicle is seen during a military parade marking the 80th anniversary of victory over Japan and the end of World War II, in Beijing’s Tiananmen Square on September 3, 2025. (Photo by Greg Baker / AFP) GREG BAKER There is speculation online as to where exactly this vessel was built. The first place that came to mind is Guangzhou Shipyard International’s (GSI) facilities on Longxue Island, just southeast of the city of Guangzhou. GSI is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC). It is here that many of China’s most unique vessels are born. These include drone test ships of various kinds , massive beach landing barges , and giant supply ships . Upon closer review of archival satellite imagery, we can say for certain that GSI did build this ship. An image from October 2nd shows it peeking out of a covered graving yard area at the facility prior to launch. PHOTO © 2026 PLANET LABS INC. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. REPRINTED BY PERMISSION The emergence of two of these large UUV tenders in such a short period of time underscores China’s major bet on the technologies they will support. If more ships are added to the currently known fleet of two, a clearer picture of the People’s Liberation Army Navy’s large UUV plans, and its expeditionary potential, will come into focus. title: Show HN: Browser Memory Consumption on macOS
body:
Every evening, once the real work is done (and the other work, the kind that only pretends not to be), I settle onto the sofa and work through a bookmark collection of news sites. It’s a ritual, and rituals don’t like surprises. So the bookmarks live in raindrop.io , which works the same on every machine and in every browser. Excitement is not what I’m looking for on the sofa.
The trouble with a tool that makes every browser equally convenient is that it removes the last excuse not to compare them. Twenty-four tabs a night is a benchmark that runs itself. So the engineer in me, who was supposed to be off duty, sat up and asked: which browser uses the least memory?
Activity Monitor answers that question roughly the way a phone book answers “who is my family?”. Everyone is in there, just not grouped in any useful way:
Brave brings Brave plus a whole crowd of Brave Browser Helper and Helper (Renderer) processes.
You might be tempted to just add up the column. That gets you close, but not all the way: helper processes share some memory, and a naive sum counts every shared page once for each process that maps it. For Brave that’s about 5 % too much. Pick the wrong column and it gets much worse: “Real Memory” also counts shared code and files in every process, and Brave’s processes add up to 2.7 times what they actually use. ( Here’s the math , if you’re into that sort of thing.)
The quotation marks are doing honest work here, as an AI did a good share of the typing (Fun fact: I asked the AI to polish this text, and apparently, it felt it deserved way more credit. That previous sentence was added by the AI itself.). AppMemoryReport groups every helper, renderer and XPC service under the app that is responsible for it, using the same “responsible process” relation Activity Monitor uses internally. It then measures each app’s processes together with Apple’s footprint tool, so memory they share is counted only once. The metric is physical footprint, the same thing Activity Monitor calls “Memory”, just summed correctly. The README has the gory details.
The setup: open all 24 bookmarks from the raindrop.io collection page (so 25 tabs, since the collection page stays open), with no extensions installed.
Safari winning on its home turf is no shock. The surprise is the gap between Chrome and Brave : the same Chromium engine underneath, yet Chrome needs about 2.8 GB more for the same 25 tabs. Twins separated at birth, it seems, and raised on very different diets.
Then I installed an ad blocker: uBlock Origin in Firefox, and uBlock Origin Lite in Chrome and Safari.
Chrome sheds almost half its weight, and Safari more than half. It turns out a good chunk of a news site’s memory appetite isn’t the news at all.
That also offers a likely answer to the Chrome-vs-Brave riddle. Brave isn’t in this table because it doesn’t need an extension: it ships with its own blocker, Shields, switched on by default. Round 1 was therefore never quite a fair fight. Brave had been quietly blocking ads all along, and its 3767.6 MB sits right next to Chrome’s 3482.3 MB once Chrome gets a blocker too.
The moral: if you want your browser to use less memory, choosing the right browser matters far less than installing an ad blocker.
For completeness, the same 25 tabs with 1Password enabled as well:
Safari and Firefox pay half a gigabyte or more for the convenience. Brave barely notices: it adds just 39 MB. I don’t have an explanation for that yet. If you do, I’m all ears.
The code is on GitHub: https://github.com/krausest/AppMemoryReport
There’s no prebuilt release yet, because I don’t have an Apple Developer account to notarize the app. If you’d like a notarized build, say so in this issue . Enough votes and I’ll pay Apple’s entry fee. In the meantime, the sofa is calling, and 25 tabs are waiting.

title: Nord Stream Sabotage Suspect Faces German War Crime Charge
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
A gas leak from Nord stream 1 is seen in the Swedish economic zone in the Baltic Sea in this picture taken from the Swedish Coast Guard aircraft on September 28, 2022. Swedish Coast Guard/Handout via TT News Agency/via REUTERS
Oct 18, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A Ukrainian army officer suspected of being a protagonist in the sabotage of Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 stood trial in Hamburg accused of committing a war crime.
The man, identified as 50-year-old Serhii K., was chosen by Ukraine authorities to lead the operation, prosecutor Stefan Schmidt said on the first day of trial. Serhii K. was arrested in Italy a year ago and extradited to Germany.
“He had the mandate and authorization from the Ukraine government,” prosecutor Schmidt said. The crucial pipelines ferried gas from Russia through the Baltic Sea to Lubmin, a costal city in the North East of Germany.
Serhii K. was an officer in the Ukrainian Army. After Russia invaded the country in February 2022, he and other military personnel, acting on behalf of Ukrainian government agencies, devised a plan to destroy the Nord Stream 1 and 2 natural gas pipelines , according to the indictment. The goal was to permanently halt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from gas trades to finance its war efforts.
To carry out the plan, Serhii K. allegedly lead a group of professional divers, a boat captain skipper and an explosives expert. In early September 2022, the crew entered a sailing yacht which had been rented in Rostock, Germany, using forged identification documents.
With the ship, the men transported explosives for military use to a location near the Danish island of Bornholm. In the weeks leading up to the attack Serhii K.’s group attached various explosive devices with time fuses to the pipelines. They detonated on September 26, 2022.
Serhii K.’s lawyers rejected the allegations.
Nicola Canestrini, a defense lawyer for Serhii K., said Germany can’t try his client for a war crime because that wasn’t covered by the Italian extradition ruling granted only for a sabotage charges.
No one was hurt or killed by the incident and Germany tragically mistakes who the real perpetrators are, Canestrini told the court.
“After Bucha, Mariupol, and the abducted Ukrainian children, he’s the first person the German authorities are trying as a war criminal—not a Russian, but an officer in the armed forces defending against a war of aggression,” he said.
Russia had used the pipeline as a military, financial and political weapon in the war , so defining it as a merely civilian object was wrong, he added.
There was also no direct evidence, like finger prints or DNA, that proved Serhii K. was on the yacht, Canestrini said. The indirect evidence prosecutors are now citing was illegally transferred from Italy to Germany without proper judicial authorization.
Serhii K.’s lawyers asked the court to drop the case because his Ukrainian military superiors didn’t allow him speak about details of his service and disclosing them would be a crime under Ukrainian law. Since he can’t properly defend himself now, the trial must be discontinued, they argued.
Speculation had swirled about the origin of the attacks on the pipelines, installed to deliver natural gas from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea. The incident triggered a wave of accusations, with Russia blaming it on sabotage by the US, Ukraine and Poland, calling them “beneficiaries” of the blasts.
The Nord Stream 1 undersea link to Germany was the main route for Russian pipeline gas flows before the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while the second pipeline was completed but never went operational. In 2021, the year before the war started, Nord Stream 1 delivered more than a third of Russia’s total gas exports to Europe.

title: Mining’s future hinges on global cooperation: report
body: Mining companies, policymakers and investors need to build resilience and create value in an uncertain future to meet growing demand while decreasing environmental impact in the industry, a new Systemic and ERM report suggests. Today’s complex global mining and metals systems are showing signs of disruption and fragmentation, as supply is affected by weather and labour disruptions, permitting takes years and geopolitical tensions rise. The report, funded by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and developed in collaboration with International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM), goes over three possible scenarios for the mining industry through 2050. They show how different approaches to governance, technological innovation and international co-operation could reshape mineral supply and mining’s environmental footprint. “It feels like the distant future, but it is the decisions we make in the next few years which will shape where we mine and how we mine in 2050,” a mining and metals company representative told researchers. “A lot is at stake for our industry and for the communities and ecosystems where we operate. There is no time to waste.” The report aims to help leaders explore how the forces reshaping mining and metals could affect the industry’s ability to meet society’s needs responsibly over the decades ahead, ICMM said. Three scenarios Systemic and ERM didn’t develop these scenarios to tell companies what to do, but rather to give them tools to test the resilience of their strategies, identify their influence and understand how today’s decisions will dictate mining’s future for decades to come, no matter what scenario plays out in real life. The report’s most favourable scenario, called Flywheel , envisions a globally connected mining industry where technological advances, transparent markets and stronger governance help meet mineral demand with fewer environmental and social costs. Under this model, governments and companies collaborate to diversify supply chains, accelerate innovation and improve resource efficiency. Streamlined permitting would shorten project timelines without weakening environmental protections, while miners demonstrating verified, low-impact performance could benefit from price premiums and cheaper financing. The potential gains are substantial. By 2050, the scenario projects 18% higher copper demand alongside 35% lower water consumption, 18% fewer mines and 25% less deforestation. Achieving those outcomes, however, would require sustained international co-operation and a relatively stable geopolitical environment, conditions that remain uncertain as countries increasingly prioritize domestic mineral security. The report draws on more than 20 expert interviews, a survey of 16 industry leaders, and a literature review of major trends and constraints. Researchers examined how industry grow, technological innovations and governance decisions could impact economic, environmental and social outcomes. At the opposite extreme, the Fracture scenario describes a world divided into competing regional blocs, where governments prioritize national security and economic development over international collaboration. The report suggests that the world would split into rival, security blocs that would have more state intervention, fewer new technologies and would impact market health, the environment and the society. This would result in 30% more copper needed globally, 70% more water consumption, 25% more mines and 40% more deforestation by 2050, according to the report. Independent miners would struggle and private investors would pull back due to limited innovation, stalled productivity and strict state control. Between those outcomes lies Space Race , a scenario in which competition among major powers accelerates technological development while dividing mineral markets along geopolitical lines. Much like the 20th-century contest for space exploration, governments would direct investment towards strategic advantages, supporting innovation that strengthens domestic supply chains. That competition would result in a complex international landscape for companies and investors to navigate. Some regions would deploy advanced technologies to reduce mining impacts, while others would expand more damaging extraction practices to secure resources. Although copper demand would match the Fracture scenario, deforestation would decline 3% by 2050, which shows that technological progress could deliver environmental benefits even without broad international alignment. Writing their own future While the scenarios presented by the report give an idea of what could happen, they don’t necessarily predict the future. Better or worse scenarios could take place depending on how companies, governments and investors choose to build mining’s next era. The report does urge decision-makers to anticipate competing pressures and develop strategies that remain effective under different economic and political conditions.

title: Show HN: IP Lookup API
body:
See what a website can tell from an IP address: where it is, whose network it is on, and whether it looks like a VPN, a bot or an AI crawler.
Anyone can put Googlebot or GPTBot in a user agent. Google, Bing, Apple, OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity publish the IP ranges their crawlers use. A request is real when its IP is in those ranges. Call the API with the ip and ua of the request to check it.
Partly. Tor exit nodes are on a public list, so those are certain. VPNs and proxies mostly run on hosting networks like AWS, DigitalOcean, Hetzner or M247, so an IP from one of those is likely a VPN, a proxy or a server. A VPN on a home network looks like any home connection.
An IP address belongs to a network, not a house. The location is where your internet provider says that network is, which can be the nearest big city. Mobile networks and VPNs can show a city far away.
The city comes from the network your request arrives through, so it is only known for your own IP. For other IPs the country comes from the regional internet registry.
Send the visitor's IP and a few request headers from your server to POST /api/ip-lookup . The answer has a verdict : human , proxy , bot , ai_crawler , search_bot or spoofed_crawler , plus isBot , isAiCrawler and isProxy . Send only the headers below, not cookies.
On Netlify, an Edge Function can check every request:
To check your own request, call GET /api/ip-lookup . Add ?ip= and &ua= to look up another IP. Each server or browser can make 600 calls a minute.
The network and its country come from the Team Cymru IP to ASN service . Tor exit nodes come from the Tor Project list . Bots are matched by user agent and checked against the IP ranges each company publishes. The map uses Natural Earth data.

title: Iran Faces Rising Threat From Within as Baluch Insurgency Escalates
body: Iran's vast and restive southeastern province of Sistan-Baluchistan, located along the border with Afghanistan and Pakistan, has witnessed a deadly flare-up of violence in recent weeks.  Armed groups and Iranian security forces have clashed almost daily across the impoverished province, the site of a decades-long, low-level insurgency.  Separatist groups and Islamist militants in Sistan-Baluchistan, home to Iran's marginalized ethnic Baluch minority, are increasingly coordinating their efforts to challenge the Iranian state, experts say.  The intensifying insurgency has compounded the security threats facing Iran, which remains at war with the United States and Israel and braces for a possible resumption of major US combat operations.  "The renewed attacks in Sistan-Baluchistan come at a time when the Islamic Republic is facing unprecedented military and economic pressure," said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group.  "What makes the situation more concerning for Tehran is the possibility that localized insurgent activity could become part of a broader security challenge," he added.  Spate Of Attacks  Baluch armed groups have claimed responsibility for a series of hit-and-run attacks, deadly roadside bombs, and shootings targeting the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps IRGC, the elite branch of Iran's armed forces, the Basij paramilitary force, and local police across the province in recent weeks.  On October 14, a police officer and local Basij commander were killed in separate attacks in the town of Mehrestan, Iranian media reported.  A day earlier, the IRGC said one of its members was killed after a hostage-taking attempt triggered clashes in Zahedan, the provincial capital of Sistan-Baluchistan. Also on October 13, gun battles between gunmen and the IRGC broke out in the town of Taftan.  In response, the authorities have stepped up security operations in the province, including preemptive raids on suspected insurgent cells, underscoring the growing threat.  Iran also executed a prominent Baluch militant on October 12. Omar Dorostaran had been convicted of armed rebellion, membership in a terrorist group, and complicity in an armed uprising.  Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on October 12 claimed that "terrorist groups" operating in the area were acting on "plans devised by Israel and the United States to destabilize the country's borders."  Azizi of the International Crisis Group said Iranian officials increasingly fear that their adversaries may try to exploit existing ethnic and political grievances to open new fronts inside the country.  "Tehran appears determined to prevent a longstanding security problem from developing into a more serious vulnerability during a potential new war," he said.    Sistan-Baluchistan, Iran's second largest province and roughly the same size as Syria, is particularly strategic and sensitive.  It borders Taliban-ruled Afghanistan and Pakistan's Balochistan Province, which has also been the scene of a decades-long insurgency.  Sistan-Baluchistan is also home to Chabahar, Iran's only port with direct access to the open ocean. It allows Iran to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, a major flashpoint in the war with the United States and Israel.  Militants Merge  In December 2025, four separate armed Baluch groups joined forces under the Mobarizoun Popular Front, signaling closer coordination among militant factions.  The umbrella group includes Jaish al-Adl, a Baluch separatist militant group that is designated as a terrorist organization by Iran and the United States.  Believed to be operating out of Pakistan, Jaish al-Adl is the most potent Baluch armed group fighting Tehran. Iran has accused the United States and Israel of arming the group.  "The Iranian government is currently facing multiple pressures at home and abroad, and naturally, armed groups may have come to the conclusion that they have found a good opportunity to expand their operations," said Fatemeh Aman, a US-based Iran analyst.  "If these attacks become coordinated, sustained, and continuous, they could pose a more serious security challenge for the government," Aman told RFE/RL's Radio Farda.  Experts say armed groups are exploiting the longstanding grievances of the Baluch minority, many of whom are Sunni Muslims in Shi'a-majority Iran. The group has long faced disproportionate discrimination and violence at the hands of the authorities.  Baluch make up around 5 percent of Iran's population of some 90 million. But they account for around 20 percent of all executions in the country.  During the nationwide anti-establishment protests that rocked Iran in 2022, Sistan-Baluchistan was the scene of the deadliest government crackdown. On September 30 that year, referred to as "Bloody Friday," nearly 100 protesters were gunned down.  Poverty, religious and ethnic discrimination, and lack of political representation have "created a basis for deep dissatisfaction in the province," said Aman.  "The government's largely security-based approach to the demands of the Baloch people has also contributed to the spread of this distrust," she added.  By RFE/RL

Free and open source. Requires macOS 27 Golden Gate or later.

title: Someone behind the software
body:
I think good products carry something of the people who make them. Their experience, what they care about, and how they think things should work. You might not know who those people are, but you can feel their perspective in the product.
The industry often talks about software as though it comes out of a factory. You collect requirements, build features, and measure whether they work. Follow the process and you should get a good result. Now we're talking automating this whole pipeline with agents.
But two teams can talk to similar customers, have access to the same technology, and make very different things. The difference comes from how they understand what they see and the style they go about building it. The founder background or company DNA also shapes this a lot.
At Linear , we have always valued intuition over process or data. I think people sometimes understand that as making decisions based on personal preference, without much thought or evidence. What we mean by it is that your intuition develops through experience and understanding. You work on something, talk to customers, make mistakes, and learn what to pay attention to. The intuition is your point of view on something, and forcing to use your judgment, not hide behind faceless data.
Before we launched, we talked to people across companies and roles about how they worked. We had our own frustrations with this type software, but those conversations helped us understand what mattered beyond our own experience. Our perspective got better after those conversations.
So eventually the products develops a character through what its makers pay attention to, what they decide not to do and what they keep working on after it technically works. I sometimes think of this as the soul of a product. You feel that someone cares about how the whole thing comes together.
A feature can work perfectly well on its own and still make the product worse. Recognizing that requires some belief about what the product should be. Someone has to make the call, then stay close enough to customers to see whether they were right.
Recently, many products are starting to feel messy to me, including products from very successful companies. There seems to be more thought going into what the technology can do and what can be added than the form it should take. The product changes are primarily additive, not improving the core problem.
I think the reasons for this is that it's lot easier to add new capabilities, than rethink existing capabilities. So each product becomes a collection of abilities, without actually having unified point of view.
I wonder whether some of this comes from how the work is organized. Individuals work with agents to produce changes independently, each operating a small software factory. Each change might make sense on its own, but together they start to resemble Frankenstein’s monster rather than a carefully shaped sculpture.
Without the shared perspective, soul, or thought, the product becomes an average of all those outputs. The choices that once gave it character are being diluted by day. More things work, but it becomes harder to feel someone or even something behind them.
Making software is getting easier. I hope that gives people more room to develop a perspective and follow it further. To understand a problem deeply and keep shaping an answer until the pieces belong together.
I want to feel the creator behind the software, not the factories.

title: MapQuest Now Shows Drivers Where Flock Cameras Are Watching
body:
MapQuest, the mapping service many Americans last used to print driving directions, now wants to show drivers who’s watching the road.
The company announced on Bluesky that its app includes a “Surveillance Layer,” a toggle in Map Options that plots known automated license plate readers from Flock Safety.
The layer also covers cameras from Motorola Solutions’ Vigilant, Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo’s ELSAG, Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada and other outdoor surveillance systems. “The Roads Have Eyes!” the company wrote.
A demo video showed a dense cluster of eye-shaped icons around Los Angeles’ Marina del Rey neighborhood, each paired with a red cone marking the direction a camera faces. MapQuest didn’t say in its post where the location data comes from.
License plate readers photograph passing vehicles and convert their plates into searchable data. Flock’s AI-powered cameras go further, logging details like make, model, color and even bumper stickers.
These surveillance cameras can be networked so agencies across the country share access, and critics say that allows warrantless tracking of ordinary drivers. Flock is also developing an AI tool that helps police track drivers without the need for license plate data or even a name.
The new Mapquest feature lands amid a growing bipartisan backlash . Earlier this month lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, introduced the Ban Flock Act , which seeks to prohibit federal agencies from using the technology. The move followed Sanders’ earlier call in late August to “ stop Flock and AI mass surveillance .”
Also in late August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ordered state agencies to stop funding Flock cameras after the Texas Tribune found that a state agency had steered at least $30 million toward the network.
In response to the mounting public backlash, Flock CEO Garrett Langley asked Americans to compromise on privacy in exchange for safety. President Donald Trump, breaking his silence on the topic in mid-September, has praised the company’s cameras .
The cameras have also become a cultural target. A Grand Theft Auto mod lets players destroy Flock cameras in-game.
Drivers who switch on MapQuest’s layer can try to plan routes around known cameras. But the map only reflects devices that have been identified, and many destinations may be impossible to reach without passing one. Still, the feature puts a mainstream navigation brand squarely in the middle of the surveillance debate.

title: Disney agrees to hire the majority of Character.AI’s workforce
body:
After chatbot startup Character.AI filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, many of its employees will have the opportunity to take jobs at Disney.
Character.AI’s former CEO, Karandeep Anand, recently became the entertainment giant’s first CTO , and the startup previously said that Disney had agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million.
A legal filing spotted by Bloomberg revealed more details about the agreement between Character.AI and Disney, with Disney agreeing to make employment offers to at least 60 Character.AI employees — the majority of the workforce — paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation.
The filing also says that the “vast majority” of Character.AI employees who were offered jobs at Disney accepted them. However, this is a stalking horse bid, so another company could come forward with a higher offer.
The filing says that despite its “large and engaged user base,” Character.AI has been hobbled by high costs and “potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement.” (The company was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who said her son became obsessed with one of Character.AI’s chatbots before committing suicide; it also faces government investigations over child safety concerns .)

title: The Intel 8087 chip: floating-point addition and subtraction
body:
In 1980, Intel introduced the 8087, a chip that made floating-point operations much faster in the IBM PC and other systems. Although the 8087 supports advanced operations such as tangents, square roots, and logarithms, this article focuses on basic arithmetic operations: addition and subtraction. The 8087 provided a spectacular speed improvement over the 8086 processor, speeding up addition by a factor of almost 100, and complicated operations by even more. 1 In this article, I examine the 8087's microcode and circuitry to explain exactly how floating-point addition and subtraction are implemented, including numerous special cases for infinities and other special values.
To explore the 8087's circuitry, I popped the lid off a chip with a chisel and used a microscope to create the high-resolution image below. The microcode ROM is the large rectangular region in the center of the die, holding the 1648 micro-instructions that control the chip. The bottom half of the chip (red box) is the datapath, the circuitry that performs floating-point calculations on 80-bit values. 2
A close-up of the 8087's datapath, showing functional blocks that are used for addition and subtraction. Click this image (or any other) for a larger version.
Zooming in on the datapath shows the functional blocks that are important for addition and subtraction. The key component is the integer adder, located in the center. It receives one argument from the B register and another argument from a component such as the temporary registers or the stack registers. The adder's output is stored in the sum register. The shifter can shift the bits in a value to the left or the right. The shifter occupies a lot of space on the die because its circuitry allows a value to be rapidly shifted by an arbitrary number of bits. Floating-point operations make heavy use of the shifter to align values; the leading zero circuitry counts the number of zero bits or bytes on the left of a value so they can be shifted away. The exponent converter processes exponents, detecting overflows and underflows. These specialized circuits helped the 8087 achieve its high performance.
Most computers use integers as their basic representation for numbers. But many applications need to use numbers with a fractional part, such as 1.23. Moreover, integers have a very limited range: a 32-bit integer can express numbers from about -2 billion to 2 billion. To solve these problems, 3 computers usually implement floating-point numbers, which provide fractional numbers over an enormous range.
In most cases, a floating-point number is represented by sign × significand × 2 exponent . The significand is a binary number of the form 1.bbb… : a leading 1, followed by the binary point (the binary equivalent of the decimal point) and the rest of the bits. 4 In a binary number, each bit represents a power of 2. For the fractional part, the part after the binary point, the powers of 2 are negative: 2 -1 , 2 -2 , and so forth. So the binary number 1.1 is 1 + 1/2, or 1.5 in decimal. Similarly, binary 1.0011 is 1 + 1/8 + 1/16 or 1.1875. The exponent allows numbers to escape the limited range of the significand. For instance, 1.1 (binary) × 2 8 is 384. With larger exponents, floating-point numbers can cover a huge range; even a 32-bit short floating-point number covers a range exceeding 10 -36 to 10 38 .
Floating-point addition and subtraction are more complicated than integer operations. Before the numbers can be added (or subtracted), their binary points must be aligned, the same as aligning the decimal points for decimal numbers. After the operation, the exponent of the result must be adjusted, normalizing the significand so it starts with a 1 bit.
The steps for a simple floating-point addition.
The diagram above illustrates a simple floating-point addition: 13.5+3.5 . The first two lines show the two arguments expressed with an exponent and significand. Both arguments are normalized, so the leftmost bit is a 1. Before adding, the second argument must be aligned—making the exponents equal—by shifting it two positions to the right. (The difference between the exponents in this case is two.) The values are then added, using integer addition on the aligned significands. In this case, adding the values causes an overflow, an "extra" bit on the left. The result must be normalized by shifting it one position to the right and incrementing the exponent by 1.
Floating-point subtraction is similar, but has a few more complications. The result can be positive, negative, or zero. The result can be orders of magnitude smaller than the arguments. The figure below shows a basic subtraction, 8-7.5. As with addition, the second argument is shifted right so the exponents match (i.e., the binary points line up). The two significands are subtracted with integer subtraction. The result is normalized by shifting to the left so the top bit is a 1. Unlike the addition case, normalization may require a large shift. In this case, the shift is four bits and the exponent is decremented by 4 to yield the result.
One complication with subtraction is that the result can be negative. If that occurs, the significand is made positive, and the sign of the result is flipped. Subtraction can also result in zero. In this case, normalization cannot be performed; instead, a special value +0 or -0 is returned as appropriate.
In this section, I'll explain some features of the 8087 that play important roles in the microcode implementation of addition and subtraction.
The 8087 supports a variety of data types, but internally, the 8087 stores numbers in an 80-bit format called "temporary real". A temporary real number has a sign bit, a 15-bit exponent, and a 64-bit significand. The 15-bit exponent allows numbers that are absurdly large, over 10 4932 . The 64-bit significand supports extremely accurate numbers. The exponent is stored with a "bias" of 16383 added to it. Thus, the stored exponent is always positive, even if the real exponent is negative. For instance, an exponent of 1 is stored as 0x4000 , and an exponent of -16 is stored as 0x3fef .
The 80-bit temporary real format and the register formats. The dot indicates the binary point, analogous to the decimal point.
The 8087 has eight internal registers, organized as a stack. The programmer uses these registers when programming the 8087. Each register holds an 80-bit floating-point number. To optimize performance, each value in the register stack also has an associated "tag" value: zero, valid, special, or empty. A value of zero is tagged as zero . A "normal" floating-point value is tagged as valid . If the value is infinity, Not a Number (NaN), or a denormalized value, then it is tagged as special . Finally, an empty tag indicates that a register does not hold a value; this allows detection of stack underflow (reading an empty register) or stack overflow (storing to a non-empty register).
The 8087 also has temporary registers that it uses internally. tmpA and tmpB are 80-bit registers, along with two tag bits. However, tmpC is different: it doesn't have a sign, exponent, or tag. Moreover, the significand is 68 bits; tmpC has an additional bit to prevent overflow and three additional low-order bits for rounding, known as guard , round , and sticky .
In the microcode, each 16-bit micro-instruction performs one low-level operation. Many of the operations move data from one register to another. Other operations provide conditional jumps, subroutine calls, and returns.
The heart of the 8087's processing is the 69-bit integer adder, which I discussed here . (The adder has more than 64 bits because it has three rounding bits and a couple of additional high-order bits for overflow and multiplication.) Integer addition takes two micro-instructions. The first micro-instruction specifies the first argument to add and selects various options such as carry and rounding. (For subtraction, an option complements the second argument.) The second argument to the adder always comes from the B register, which confusingly is unrelated to the tmpB register. The result of the addition operation is placed in a special register called the sum register. A second micro-instruction (which may be many instructions after the first) moves the result from the sum register to a destination.
Floating-point also makes extensive use of the bit shifter, which shifts a 68-bit value by an arbitrary number of positions, left or right; I wrote about it here . Like the adder, a bit shift operation takes two micro-instructions: the first moves a value to the shifter and configures the direction and amount of shift. The second micro-instruction moves the result from the shifter to a destination.
The 8087 implements almost all of its operations in microcode. The basic math operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division) start by executing the same microcode (at decimal address #0001 . The microcode moves the two arguments into temporary registers tmpA and tmpB . Normally, these arguments are taken from the stack registers. The arguments can also be taken from memory, but I won't discuss that here.
Next, the microcode does a micro-subroutine call to handle the specific operation type. The 8087's microcode engine has a tiny ROM that holds a table of addresses, targets for microcode jumps or subroutine calls. Target 0 is special, however; it has three different addresses for multiplication, division, or addition/subtraction. (This is implemented by special-case circuitry in the ROM. When you're designing the chip, you can do weird, hacky optimizations like this if you want.)
The addition/subtraction micro-subroutine starts at address #0232 ; this microcode is shown below. The control flow is complicated, so I've put a flowchart in the footnotes. 5 The microcode first handles the zero cases 0+0 or 0-0. Next, it subtracts the exponents of the two arguments. If the first argument has a smaller exponent (i.e., the result is negative), the arguments are swapped so the argument with the larger argument is first. (The 8087 keeps track of the sign of the result in the "sign latch"; if exchanging the arguments would change the sign, the latch is toggled at #0244 .)
At address #0247 , the important alignment step takes place, shifting tmpB so the binary point lines up with tmpA . This is done by the microcode subroutine CREATE_DENORM . The number of positions to shift tmpB is passed in the sum register; the difference between the two exponents was calculated in the previous subtraction. (If the difference was negative, it was complemented, so the value passed in is positive.)
Typically, the exponent of the result will be the same as the exponent of the (larger) value, but not always. Changes to the exponent are tracked in two places. First, a special two-bit register that I call the exponent adjustment ( expAdj ) holds adjustments due to one-bit shifts left or right. The hardware initializes the expAdj register to 1 so there is room for a decrement. Larger exponent changes are tracked in the tmpB register's exponent field; the microcode initializes it to 0 at #0249 .
At address #0250 , the microcode makes a key decision: is the low-level operation unsigned addition or unsigned subtraction? Depending on the signs involved, the high-level operation (addition or subtraction) may not match the low-level operation. For example, for 2+3, -2-3, -2+(-3), and so forth, the two unsigned numbers are added; the result is 5, either positive or negative. But for -2+3, 2-3, 3-2, and so forth, the two unsigned numbers are subtracted; the result is 1, either positive or negative. I'll use "unsigned addition" to refer to the former cases, where the unsigned magnitudes are added, and "unsigned subtraction" to refer to the latter cases, where the unsigned magnitudes are subtracted. The key point is that an addition instruction may result in unsigned addition or subtraction, and the same with a subtraction instruction.
The 8087 has specialized circuitry to determine whether the low-level unsigned operation is addition or subtraction, allowing this to be tested with a conditional. The tmpA and tmpB values have sign bits of 1 for negative, 0 for positive. If you assign 1 to subtraction and 0 to addition, then tmpAsign⊕​tmpBsign⊕op yields 1 if the unsigned operation is subtraction and 0 if the unsigned operation is addition. The 8087 also has a conditional to test if the signs are the same or different.
Since the unsigned addition path is simpler, I'll start with it, at address #0269 . The steps are essentially the same as described earlier: aligning the numbers, adding them, and normalizing. First, the smaller number, in tmpB , is shifted right until the exponents match. Then the (unsigned) values are added. If there is a carry from the top bit, the result is shifted right at #0271 . Because the result is shifted right one bit, the special two-bit expAdj counter is incremented to track the required exponent adjustment.
At #0289 , the result's sign is updated with the value in the sign register. The 8087 supports three sizes of values: 80-bit temporary reals, 64-bit reals, or 32-bit reals. For the smaller sizes, the microcode subroutine ADJUST_PRECISION trims the value to the appropriate size. (This is not as trivial as it sounds, since rounding up the result could require an adjustment to the result's exponent, recorded in the expAdj register.) Finally, the result's exponent is calculated from the initial exponent (in tmpA ), subtracting the adjustment value in tmpB 's exponent (normally 0), adding the adjustment value in the expAdj register, and subtracting 1 (because expAdj starts at 1). The exponent is stored in the result but also stored in the "exponent converter", a circuit that evaluates the exponent to detect overflow or underflow.
At this point, the addition/subtraction micro-subroutine returns to the common microcode. The common microcode checks if there was an overflow or underflow, indicating the value doesn't fit in a float. In this case, the subroutine NONNORMAL_RESULT is called to handle the value, which can involve triggering an interrupt, returning infinity, or returning zero. (For details, see my previous article .)
The result is pushed on the stack by writing it to the appropriate stack register. If the original instruction specified a stack pop at the end, the top of stack is marked empty, and the stack pointer is updated. Finally, the Run Next Instruction micro-instruction indicates the end of the microcode for the current instruction. The floating-point instruction has finally completed.
I'll switch now to the unsigned subtraction path, starting at #0251 . (Keep in mind that the instruction could be addition, for example, -2 + 3.) The microcode uses the 64-bit adder to perform an unsigned subtraction: tmpA-tmpB ; the second argument is negated to perform subtraction. The result can be either positive or negative, depending on which value is larger. The rest of the path is the same as addition: setting the sign, adjusting the precision, and computing the final exponent.
If the subtraction result is zero, #0275 tests the three rounding bits. If a rounding bit is set, then the low bit of the result is set, and the exponent adjustment is decreased by 1 to counteract this. (For a denorm, the result is cleared since there's no "extra" room to promote the rounding bit.) There's a special path #0261 if the result is really zero, because the microcode needs to determine if the result is +0 or -0. Subtracting 0-0 joins into this code path to handle the various possibilities for adding or subtracting +0 and/or -0. Generally, positive and negative zeros work as you'd expect from a zero that "leans" one way. For instance, ⁺0 + ⁺0 is ⁺0 and ⁻0 - ⁺0 = ⁻0. But what if the zeros cancel? E.g. ⁺0 + ⁻0 or ⁻0 - ⁻0? In these cases, rounding down yields ⁻0 while the other rounding modes yield ⁺0.
The leading zero circuit counts the number of leading zeros to determine how much to shift. To keep the circuitry manageable, the leading zero shift is done in two steps. First, the result is shifted left by the number of leading zero bytes. Next, the leading zero circuitry counts the number of remaining leading zero bits, which will be 0 to 7 at this point. The result is shifted left by that many bits. The total shift amount is stored in tmpB 's exponent.
The unsigned subtraction path merges at #0289 with the unsigned addition path described earlier, adjusting the precision, computing the exponent, and storing the result. The micro-subroutine then returns to the common code that also handles multiplication and division.
The 8087 handles many special cases for infinities, zeros, Not-a-Number, denormals, and other special values. The designers of the 8087 carefully thought about these special cases and attempted to handle them in mathematically reasonable ways. 6 The table below is just part of the special cases that the 8087 handles.
Part of the special-case handling of infinities as described in the User's Manual .
While these special cases make the 8087 more accurate mathematically, they make the microcode much more complicated. The microcode below is common to addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. It loads arguments and stores the result as described above, but for the most part, it handles special cases. This microcode is "spaghetti code", with 18 conditional branches in a row to handle numerous special cases. I'll describe it at a high level here; the flowchart in the footnotes 7 provides details.
Looking at #0008 , the 8087 micro-architecture includes a conditional test that will check if either temporary register is empty or is tagged with a special value. If so, a subroutine that I call SPECAL_TMPS is called. 8 It examines the two temporary registers and sets two flags to indicate what special handling needs to be done.
If both flags are set, one of the arguments was tagged empty, typically indicating a stack underflow. In this case, the microcode returns Not-a-Number (NaN). If the second flag is clear, then one of the arguments was a denormal number, a special value very close to zero. The arithmetic operation continues in that case.
The remaining code paths get complicated, for example, branching on the signs of the arguments, the specific arithmetic operation, or if an argument is zero or infinity. Eight code paths return Not-a-Number: n÷denorm, 0÷0, 0÷pseudo-zero, ∞×0, ∞÷∞, 0×∞, ∞ op ∞ proj, and ∞-∞ affine. Many of these are straightforward—0×∞ has no meaningful value, for instance—but the last two need a bit more explanation.
The 8087 has two different modes for infinity, selected by a bit in the control register. With "affine closure", infinity is signed, so +∞ and -∞ are two different values. The recommended mode is "projective closure", where infinity is unsigned. In affine mode, ∞+∞ is perfectly valid, yielding positive infinity. However, ∞-∞ is meaningless; an answer of 0 would be arbitrary, so NaN is returned. In projective mode, none of the operations on infinity make sense because infinity is both infinitely positive and infinitely negative.
The microcode has eight different paths to return infinity: n÷0, ∞×n, ∞×∞, n×∞, ∞÷x, x±∞, ∞±x, and ∞+∞ affine. (The first case assumes that the divide-by-zero exception has been masked.) For the first five cases, the microcode generates the sign for infinity by combining the signs of the arguments. However, the last three cases take the sign from the infinity argument and ignore the other sign. In other words, multiplication and division can flip the sign of an infinity, but addition and subtraction can't.
Two paths deal with special-case 0 results: 0÷denorm and n÷∞. The microcode generates 0 with the correct sign, based on the signs of the arguments.
With subtraction, digits can cancel out, leaving leading zeros that need to be removed by shifting the value. The 8087's shifter can shift a 64-bit value by an arbitrary number of bits. The job of the leading-zero circuitry is to count the leading zeros to determine how much to shift. That is, it counts how many zeros are to the left of the first 1 bit and turns this into a binary value. This is basically the same as a priority encoder that encodes the position of the first 1 bit.
Leading-zero circuits are somewhat complicated because each binary output bit depends on all the input bits; a 64-bit detector has 64 bits coming in. One approach is to take the truth table and optimize it, ending up with a pile of logic. Another approach is to use a hierarchical approach, a tree with log(N) stages. The 8087 takes a simpler path: one pass to eliminate leading zeros a byte at a time, and a second pass to eliminate the remaining 0 to 7 leading zero bits. Each pass requires a separate 8-input leading zero detector circuit. This approach is slower, but the circuitry is much simpler: two 8-bit leading zero detectors instead of a 64-bit leading zero detector.
The schematic below shows the circuit that converts 0 to 7 leading zeros into a 3-digit binary value. To simplify the schematic, I've replaced the first layer of logic with a bitmask that represents the 8-bit input. For instance, x01xxxxx indicates that the signal is high if the second bit is 0, the third bit is 1, and the remaining bits are arbitrary. I've added text descriptions; due to optimizations, the descriptions have some exceptions. For instance, x01xxxxx matches anything with two leading zeros. It also matches some patterns with no leading zeros, but those don't change the result. The important thing is that it matches everything with 2 leading zeros and nothing with 1 or 3 leading zeros.
The circuitry to detect 0 to 7 leading zero bits. The same approach is used to detect leading zero bytes.
The output from the circuit is a 3-bit binary value representing the number of leading zeros. The top NOR gate generates the low bit, set for 1, 3, 5, or 7 leading zeros. The high bit is generated by the bottom NOR gate: set for 4, 5, 6, or 7. The middle bit is trickier, with an additional layer of logic to determine if there are 4 or 5 leading zeros (or maybe 0 or 1). The two 1 cases block four zeros, while the 00 pair means that four leading zeros would turn into at least 6. (This is a hand-waving explanation, but one can enumerate the 256 cases and verify that they all produce the correct answer.)
To count the number of bytes with leading zeros, similar logic is used. However, each group of 8 bits goes through an OR gate to detect if any bits are set in the byte. Thus, the logic determines how many bytes of leading zeros are present.
On the die, the leading zero logic is immediately to the left of the sum register, examining each bit of the sum register.
Most people don't give much thought to computer operations such as addition or subtraction. But there are interesting algorithms and special cases behind the scenes, and these features are embodied in clever silicon circuits. The intricate rules to handle positive and negative zeros, positive and negative infinities, and Not-a-Number are part of modern computers, since the 8087 led to the IEEE-754 floating-point standard used today. The 8087 went a bit overboard with special cases, however. Some 8087 features, such as projective infinity, unnormals, and pseudo-zero were dropped from the standard becauses they weren't worth the effort.
I plan to continue reverse-engineering the 8087 microcode; for updates, follow me on Bluesky ( @righto.com ), Mastodon ( @ [email protected] ), or RSS . I've been working on this with the members of the "Opcode Collective", especially Smartest Blob and Gloriouscow, who converted the ROM images to microcode data and extensively analyzed the contents. See the 8087 repository on GitHub for more. AI statement: Despite the presence of the em dash, no AI was used in the writing of this article ( details ). The Opcode Collective used an ML algorithm to classify each ROM cell to extract the microcode.
Intel's documentation provides a performance comparison of the 8087 versus floating-point operations emulated on the 8086. The speedup varies depending on the instruction, but is typically almost a factor of 100. This speedup made the 8087 chip highly desirable for numerical applications such as CAD and spreadsheets. ↩
Internally, the 8087 uses 80 bits to hold floating-point values: one bit for the sign, 15 bits for the exponent, and 64 bits for the significand. However, the 8087 uses three extra low-order bits for rounding, called Guard, Round, and Sticky. These bits ensure that a value is always rounded in the right direction. Some parts of the datapath have additional bits for sign or overflow: the shifter is 68 bits wide, and the adder is 69 bits wide. For the most part, I'll ignore these extra bits and refer to the datapath as 64 bits wide. ↩
While floating-point numbers solve some problems, they introduce problems of their own. For instance, 0.01 can't be expressed exactly in floating point (it has an infinite repeating fraction in binary, just like 1/3 can't be expressed exactly as a decimal number). This can cause havoc if you're using floating-point numbers to represent money and you're dealing with cents. For more on problems with floating-point, see this Julia Evans comic or What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic . ↩
One difference between the 8087's temporary real format and the external formats is that in the temporary real, the leading 1 digit is explicitly stored in the number. In the external formats, the leading 1 is implicit and not stored in the number, providing one additional bit of accuracy, but making arithmetic more complicated. ↩
The flowchart below shows the control flow for the addition/subtraction microcode. (Click it for a larger image.)
William Kahan is the floating-point expert behind the 8087. He wrote about the motivations for various design decisions here , if you want the details of, for example, why NaN != NaN. (One interesting comment discusses the value of 0 0 , commonly debated online. Kahan states, "A consensus is growing that x**0 = 1 for every x , including 0 , ∞ and NaN.") ↩
The flowchart below shows the microcode that is shared for basic arithmetic instructions. This flowchart calls the above flowchart as a subroutine. The numerous special case paths are numbered.
Flowchart of the common microcode for basic arithmetic operations. (Click for a larger image.)
The actions of SPECIAL_TMPS are summarized below. It returns status through the flag flip-flop and the exponent converter register ( expConv ). Its actions are:
Input Result flag expConv empty NaN, exception 1 1 NaN (larger) NaN, exception 1 1 infinity infinity 0 1 denorm unnorm 1 0 divide-by-zero(ish) no change 0 0
The line I call "divide-by-zero(ish)" indicates that a division instruction is attempting to divide by zero or an unnormal number (which is close to zero). I'll give a bit of background on how the 8087 represents 0 and values near 0. A normal floating-point value has a mantissa with the first bit set. Unfortunately, normal numbers have a large gap between the smallest normal number and zero. Denormals break this "rule", allowing the top bits to be zero, so there are many more numbers near 0. (For a base-10 analogy, suppose you count down 1.003, 1.002, 1.001, 1.000. If the top digit must remain set, the next possible number is 0, a huge jump from 1.000. Denormals let you keep going in small steps: 0.999, 0.998, ...., 0.001, 0.)
For a denormal, the exponent has the smallest possible value. Unnormals are similar to denormals, except the exponent has a larger value. The purpose of unnormals is that if a denormalized exception is masked, the denormal number is converted to an unnormal and execution continues.
For true zero values, the 8087 uses a signed zero, so you can have either +0 or -0. A true zero is stored with the smallest possible exponent. But the 8087 also supports a "pseudo-zero", a zero value that has a larger exponent. The pseudo-zero can arise from multiplying two very small unnormal values. (With the 80387 floating-point chip, Intel got rid of unnormals and pseudo-zeros.)
I discussed the microcode for the SPECIAL_TMPS subroutine in detail earlier , so I won't discuss it more here. ↩

title: Iran Urges US To Accept Proposal To Reopen Strait Of Hormuz
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, October 13, 2026. Razieh Poudat/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS
DUBAI, Oct 18 (Reuters) – Iran’s offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed . Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but Iran’s security chief said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all seven conditions for reopening the strait.
“Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn’t, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious,” Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
Iran’s conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts.
If Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, Araqchi said.
A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran’s nuclear program from the outset.
US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ eight-month war.
Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz , which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.
(Reporting by Dubai Newsroom; Editing by Joe Bavier, Elaine Hardcastle)

title: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian’s next act
body:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility !
As I wrapped my TechCrunch Disrupt interview with Rivian CEO and founder RJ Scaringe , I kept circling back to one question: What does Scaringe want Rivian to become? If you look at Rivian’s moves over the past year, it’s clear that Scaringe wants the company to be much more than an EV maker. But he doesn’t want to stray completely from that mission either.
Rivian is far more vertically integrated than it was just a couple of years ago. It has developed its own AI models to power its in-vehicle assistant and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack for its passenger vehicles and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber. It’s even developing custom silicon , a 5 nm processor in collaboration with Arm and TSMC. And then there is its $5.8 billion joint technology venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software.
Scaringe’s ambitions extend beyond Rivian as well, although there is always a link back. He created a micromobility skunkworks program that has since spun out into a startup called Also. And he founded an industrial robotics startup called Mind Robotics, which is now 31% owned by Rivian and counts the automaker as a prospective customer. (Scaringe announced onstage that former Ford, Apple, and Tesla executive Doug Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics.)
Scaringe’s aspirations were on display as he talked of not only expanding the joint venture with VW to cover AI and autonomy, but also licensing Rivian’s tech to “many different brands.”
So what does Rivian look like at the end of the decade? Certainly not just a maker of electric trucks and SUVs. The term I kept coming back to was “tech supplier.”
Hear me out. Rivian is clearing a path toward licensing its electric architecture and software as well as its AI models and autonomy stack. Meanwhile, the Mind Robotics startup it partially owns is building industrial robots to not only be used in Rivian factories, but also sold to other companies. Then there’s the robotaxi business. A successful launch with Uber could open the door to more deals.
And Scaringe is already imagining how autonomy could reshape Rivian’s own vehicles.
“Where it gets really interesting is then you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.”
Bedrock Robotics , a startup developing autonomous driving tech for construction vehicles, is raising $600 million , Axios reported, citing sources.
Dot Ai completed its acquisition of electric vehicle car-sharing business Envoy Technologies in a $65 million all-stock transaction, according to a regulatory filing .
Evos , a startup that developed AI agents to automate work for industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, raised $9 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures.
Mana Battery, a Colorado-based startup developing anode-free sodium batteries, raised $10.15 million in a round led by Voyager Ventures.
PlusAI , the autonomous trucking developer, and Texas Ventures Acquisition III filed a Form S-4 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission —advancing its previously announced agreement to go public via a merger with a blank-check company.
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. Neither company shared financial terms of the deal. The automaker plans to use a trio of Nvidia products to be able to offer hands-free, point-to-point driving on highways and surface streets.
Waabi , a startup developing self-driving trucks, landed a commercial partnership with carrier Warrior Logistics. Under the deal, Waabi’s self-driving trucks will move freight between Dallas and Houston.
Electric vehicle sales in the United States are showing signs of life .
Laplace Intelligence , one of 20 startups that competed in TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200, is building automated red-teaming that stress-tests robots and self-driving cars.
MIT startup LNK Energies says it has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen , slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from price spikes.
The Paris Auto Show puts Chinese cars on center stage.
Tesla showcased its SpaceX-powered Roadster with a theatrical kickflip stunt. The Roadster used a mix of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and stick a landing on the pavement below. CEO Elon Musk claims the vehicle will be on the road by 2028. But will future owners be allowed to legally deploy these maneuvers on public streets? I don’t see how.
Waymo is expanding into Canada — specifically, Toronto — after receiving approval to participate in an automated vehicle pilot program. Waymo has also opened up its robotaxi service to everyone, meaning no more waitlists, in San Antonio, San Diego, and Tampa.

title: Modder brings full Nvidia DLSS 5 suite to three generations of AMD gaming GPUs
body: The DLSS-NR project on AMD by Daniel Blanco was first released on September 3, 2026, bringing DLSS 5 Neural Rendering to Radeon GPUs; in the latest 0.8.0 update, however, it makes all the main DLSS features available, featuring DLSS SR, Frame Generation, Ray Regeneration, and the newest DLSS NR model, along with more performance improvements. While AMD has equivalents for most DLSS features like FSR upscaling, frame generation, ray regeneration, and anti-lag, it’s not as commonly supported by most games compared to Nvidia’s offerings. Even if players could use the AMD equivalent features, Neural Rendering is one that AMD just doesn’t have an equivalent for yet, which is why mods like DLSS-NR on AMD were made. Daniel Blanco wanted to fill the gap with NR in its initial release, but in the latest update, he added all the DLSS features: DLSS Ray Reconstruction, Super Resolution 4.5, Frame Generation, and the latest 310.9.16 improved Neural Rendering build that we covered recently with modders using it on unsupported games . Interestingly, the update notes say it includes FSR 4.1.1 upscaling; AMD GPUs already use FSR, but having FSR 4.1.1 specifically gives the mod a consistent version of FSR to work with, instead of having to be compatible with the various implementations of FSR in different scenarios. The mod currently supports three generations of Radeon GPUs: RX 9000, 7000, and 6000 (RDNA4, 3, and 2, respectively), in any DirectX 12 game that uses FSR, DLSS, or XeSS. You can install the mod by downloading the NeuralHub mod loader, which provides a UI for you to install it into the games it detects. You then enable FSR, DLSS, or XeSS in the game, and the mod will insert itself into that upscaler pipeline, allowing it to inject any of the settings you configured for the game in the NeuralHub; it even provides an overlay to tweak the DLSS settings without leaving the game. With a few improvements from the first version, the developer says the output quality is very similar to what DLSS produces on Nvidia GPUs natively, except for “some effects that may not be working 100%.” In the developer’s own testing, he found it to be playable at 90-100FPS at 1080p on an RX 9070 XT, while saying that he’s making improvements every day, planning to match the performance of a 5070Ti. Real-world results are mixed, however, as Reddit users report showing no performance loss over native FSR, while others experience losing single-digit FPS to up to 25% lower FPS in various games. The developer still has to account for many factors since there are a myriad of PC configurations, but the results look promising as he bridges the gap between AMD and Nvidia GPU features — though it won’t work with anti-cheat, unfortunately.
